title: Two ideas, one question: how to tell explanations apart

summary.text: A steel tumbler of ice water is wet on the outside. One friend says the water leaked through the steel. Another says it came from the air. Both friends saw exactly the same drops. In this unit your child learns to split what they see from what they think it means. They list the rival ideas, and ask the one question that the ideas answer differently. They test the tumbler with coloured water, search for a pattern in arm spans and heights, and meet Jocelyn Bell, who used the same kind of question to find a signal from space.
summary.art: A steel tumbler of ice water on a plate in a kitchen, covered in small drops on the outside, with two children pointing at it and two thought bubbles showing different ideas.

intro.hook: Fill a steel tumbler with ice water and wait ten minutes. The outside is wet. Nobody poured water there. Where did it come from?
intro.text: Ask three people and you may hear three answers. One says it leaked through the steel. One says it came from the ice. One says it came out of the air. All three looked at the same wet tumbler. They saw the same drops and told three different stories. In this unit you learn how to tell stories apart. You ask what each story would predict, and then you look for the one result that the stories disagree about.
intro.art: Three people around a wet steel tumbler, each with a speech bubble: it leaked, it is from the ice, it is from the air.

outcomes: I can tell what I saw (an observation) from what I think it means (an inference).
I can write down two or more rival explanations for something I noticed.
I can ask a deciding question, one that two explanations would answer differently.
I can write a prediction as an if-then sentence for each explanation, and say what result would show an idea wrong.
I can explain why drops form on the outside of a cold tumbler, and how I tested it.
I can look for a pattern by measuring many people or things, and say what a pattern does and does not show.
I can choose a way of finding out that suits my question: a fair test, a pattern search, a long watch, or looking it up.
I can say what to do when a result surprises me.

terms.meaning: What you notice with your senses or with a tool, without adding why. Anyone standing beside you can check it.
terms.example: The outside of the steel tumbler is covered in small clear drops.
terms.art: A child looking closely at a wet steel tumbler, with a magnifying glass over the drops.

terms.meaning: A guess or conclusion you work out from what you noticed. It goes beyond what you saw, so it can be wrong.
terms.example: The water leaked through the steel. Nobody saw water crossing the steel, so this is an inference.
terms.art: A thought bubble above a wet tumbler showing water crossing the steel wall.

terms.meaning: A statement of why or how something happens.
terms.example: The drops come from water in the air that turned to liquid on the cold steel.
terms.art: A speech bubble over a tumbler with an arrow from the air to the drops.

terms.meaning: Two or more explanations for the same thing you saw. They cannot all be right, so you have to find a way to choose between them.
terms.example: Leaked through the steel and came out of the air are rival explanations for the drops.
terms.art: Two arrows pointing to the same wet tumbler from two different ideas.

terms.meaning: The scientists' word for an explanation that you can test. A hypothesis has to be something that could turn out wrong.
terms.example: The drops come from the air is a hypothesis. We can colour the water inside and see whether the drops are coloured.
terms.art: A card with the words 'The drops come from the air' and a tick-box marked 'test it'.

terms.meaning: What you expect to see if an idea is true. A good prediction is written as an if-then sentence, before the test.
terms.example: If the water leaked through the steel, then the drops on the outside will be the colour of the water inside.
terms.art: A page with the words 'If ... then ...' written in a notebook.

terms.meaning: What you saw or measured that counts for or against an idea. Evidence is not the same as the idea.
terms.example: The drops were clear while the water inside was yellow. That is evidence against 'it leaked through'.
terms.art: A yellow tumbler with clear drops on the outside, and an arrow pointing to the drops.

terms.meaning: A question that two explanations answer differently. When you get the answer, one explanation is in trouble.
terms.example: Is the water on the outside the same colour as the water inside? Leaking says yes, and the air idea says no.
terms.art: A fork in a path, each branch labelled with one explanation, and a question mark at the fork.

terms.meaning: Water as an invisible gas, mixed into the air. There is some in the air of every room, even when it feels dry.
terms.example: Wet clothes on a line dry because the water leaves them and goes into the air as vapour.
terms.art: Tiny dots drifting upward from a wet cloth on a line, labelled water vapour.

terms.meaning: Water vapour turning back into tiny drops of liquid water when it touches something cold.
terms.example: The mist on a mirror after a hot shower, and the drops on a cold tumbler, are condensation.
terms.art: A cold tumbler with dots from the air landing on its wall and joining into drops.

terms.meaning: Something that repeats or goes together in the same way in many cases.
terms.example: In most families, the taller people also have the longer arm spans.
terms.art: Six people standing in a row, with a line joining their heights to their arm spans.

terms.meaning: The distance from the tip of one middle finger to the tip of the other, when your arms are stretched out wide.
terms.example: A girl who is 130 centimetres tall may have an arm span of about 130 centimetres too.
terms.art: A child standing against a wall with arms stretched wide and a tape measure along them.

terms.meaning: The small wobble in any measurement, from where you hold the tape, how you read it, or how still the person stands. It is not the same as a mistake.
terms.example: Two people measure the same child and get 131 and 133 centimetres. The 2 centimetres is measurement error.
terms.art: Two hands holding a tape measure at slightly different places on the same child.

terms.meaning: The group of people or things you measure, in order to learn about a much bigger group.
terms.example: Measuring eight people from your street is a sample of everyone in your city.
terms.art: Eight small figures chosen from a big crowd and circled.

terms.meaning: A result that does not match what your idea predicted. It is information. It is not a failure.
terms.example: You thought the warm tumbler would sweat, but it stayed dry. That tells you something about warm air and cold steel.
terms.art: A dry warm tumbler beside a wet cold tumbler, with an exclamation mark between them.

terms.meaning: A pattern in measurements that carries real information, such as a regular beat.
terms.example: A radio hiss that comes back at the same time every evening is a signal.
terms.art: A wavy line with a clear regular bump repeating, labelled signal.

terms.meaning: Random wobble in measurements that carries no message.
terms.example: The crackle on a radio when a mixer grinder is switched on nearby is noise.
terms.art: A messy scribble line beside a clean regular line.

terms.meaning: Unwanted noise from things nearby, which gets mixed into a measurement.
terms.example: A phone buzzing near a speaker is interference.
terms.art: A speaker with a phone next to it and zigzag lines between them.

terms.meaning: A star that has collapsed into a tiny, spinning ball and sends out a beam that sweeps past the Earth like a lighthouse, so we get a pulse each turn.
terms.example: The first pulsar was found by Jocelyn Bell in 1967 as a regular blip on a paper chart.
terms.art: A tiny bright star with two beams sweeping through space like a lighthouse.

explanations.concept: What I saw and what I think it means
explanations.definition: An observation is what you can see, hear, touch, smell or measure. An inference is what you work out from it. They are different, and we keep them apart.
explanations.description: Look at a cold tumbler with small clear drops on the outside. 'There are small clear drops on the outside' is an observation. Anyone standing beside you can check it. 'The water leaked through the steel' is an inference. It sounds like something you saw, but nobody saw water cross the steel. Words like 'because', 'leaked', 'made' and 'wants' are clues that an inference has slipped in. Inferences are not bad. Science is full of them. The trouble starts when we forget we made one. Then we stop asking whether it is right. A good habit is to write two columns, 'I saw' and 'I think', and move each sentence into the right one.
examples: A crow turns their head towards our plate. That is an observation. 'The crow is hungry' is an inference.
A friend is not smiling. That is an observation. 'She is angry with me' is an inference. She may only be tired.
The fan blades turn slowly. That is an observation. 'The fan is about to break' is an inference.
explanations.art: A page split in two columns headed I saw and I think, with sentences about a wet tumbler sorted into them.

explanations.concept: Rival explanations: many stories for one sight
explanations.definition: Rival explanations are different explanations for the same observation. Usually at most one of them is right.
explanations.description: One sight can have many stories. A wet patch appears on the wall under the bathroom. Is it a leaking pipe? Is it rain coming through the terrace? Is it damp from the cold water pipe? Each story fits the wet patch. So the wet patch alone cannot choose between them. This is why we write the rival explanations down side by side before we test anything. It stops us falling in love with the first story we thought of. It also reminds us to look for a fourth story, because the right one is sometimes the one nobody has said yet.
examples: Drops on a cold tumbler: the water leaked through, it came out of the air, or it was my own wet hand.
A dosa batter rises overnight: it was the warm kitchen, the time, or the microbes already in the batter.
A crow keeps visiting the balcony: for the water pot, for the dry rice, or because someone feeds them.
explanations.art: Three arrows from one wet wall patch to three drawings of possible causes: a pipe, rain and a cold pipe.

explanations.concept: A deciding question tells two ideas apart
explanations.definition: A deciding question is a question that two explanations answer differently. Whichever answer you get, at least one explanation is in trouble.
explanations.description: Watching more of the same thing often cannot choose between two ideas, because both ideas fit. You need a question where the ideas disagree. For the tumbler, ask: what colour will the drops be if the water inside is coloured? If the water leaked through the steel, the drops will be coloured. If the water came from the air, the drops will be clear. The ideas disagree, so the colour decides. To find a deciding question, take each idea in turn and ask: if this were true, what else would I see, that the other idea would not give me?
examples: Bell or dusk: do the pigeons still leave on an evening when the bell does not ring?
Leak or air: is the water on the outside the same colour as the water inside?
Wet patch from a pipe or from rain: does the patch grow on a dry day?
explanations.art: A signpost at a fork in a path, each arm pointing to one idea, with a question on the post.

explanations.definition: A prediction written as 'If this idea is true, then I will see this' is a prediction you can check. It names the idea and the result together.
explanations.description: Writing the prediction before the test matters. After a result arrives, it is easy to believe we expected it all along. The if-then shape keeps us honest, because it ties each result to one idea. Write one sentence for each idea, so that two ideas give two sentences. Make them as clear as you can, with a colour, a number or a time, so that nobody can argue afterwards about what it meant. If both sentences would give the same result, the test cannot choose between them. Go back and find a better deciding question.
examples: If the water leaked through the steel, then the drops will be yellow when the water inside is yellow.
If the pigeons leave because of the bell, then they will stay when the bell does not ring.
If arm span is the same as height, then the difference between the two will be close to zero for everyone.
explanations.art: A notebook page with two if-then sentences written side by side and a blank space for the result.

explanations.concept: An idea you can test must be able to fail
explanations.definition: A testable idea says something that could turn out wrong. If no result could ever show an idea wrong, nobody can use a test to learn about it.
explanations.description: Suppose someone says: the drops are made by a tiny invisible helper who hides whenever we look. Whatever we see, the helper explains it. If the drops are clear, the helper made them clear. If they are yellow, the helper made them yellow. An idea that fits every possible result tells us nothing about this tumbler. It might even be true, but we cannot test it. A good scientific idea sticks its neck out. It says: if I am right, you will see this. If you do not see it, I am wrong. That is what makes it useful, because it can be checked by anyone.
examples: 'The drops come from the air' sticks its neck out. A coloured-water test could show it wrong.
'Pigeons leave because of the bell' sticks its neck out. A bell-free evening could show it wrong.
'Mangoes taste best because that is how mangoes are' cannot be tested, because no result could ever show it wrong.
explanations.art: A boxer's head sticking out of a box labelled testable idea, next to a closed box labelled can never be wrong.

explanations.definition: Different questions need different ways of finding out. The main ways are a fair test, a pattern search, a long watch, looking it up or asking, and a model.
explanations.description: A fair test changes one thing and keeps the rest the same. Use it for 'what happens if I change this?' A pattern search measures many people or things and looks for what goes together. Use it for 'do taller people have longer arms?' A long watch looks at the same thing again and again over time. Use it for 'when does the streetlight come on?' Looking it up or asking an expert answers questions you cannot test at home, such as how far away the Sun is. A model is a drawing, a toy or a computer program that copies the real thing, so you can try ideas safely. Many investigations use more than one way.
examples: Does more salt make a potato float? A fair test, changing the amount of salt.
Do taller people have longer feet? A pattern search across many people.
How far away is the Moon? Look it up, because we cannot test it at home.
explanations.art: Five small pictures in a row: a balance for a fair test, a row of people for a pattern, a clock for a long watch, a book for looking it up, and a toy model.

explanations.concept: Why drops form on the outside of a cold tumbler
explanations.definition: The air around us holds invisible water called water vapour. When air touches something cold, some of its vapour turns into tiny drops of liquid water. This is called condensation.
explanations.description: Air is a mix of gases, and one of them is water vapour. Warmer air can hold more vapour than colder air. When air touches the cold steel, the air right next to the steel cools. It can no longer hold all its vapour as a gas. Some of the vapour turns into liquid and lands on the steel as tiny drops. The drops grow and join. The water does not come from inside the tumbler. The steel is a closed wall, and coloured water inside does not cross it. A warm tumbler does not sweat, because the air next to it stays warm. On a very dry day the drops come slowly, because there is less vapour to collect.
examples: A cold bottle taken from the fridge is wet within minutes, though its cap is shut tight.
Mist forms on a bathroom mirror after a hot shower, because the warm moist air touches the cooler glass.
On a very dry winter day a cold tumbler may stay almost dry for a long time, because there is little vapour to collect.
explanations.art: A cross-section of a cold steel tumbler with tiny dots of water vapour in the air landing on its outer wall and growing into drops, and clear water on the inside.

explanations.concept: Looking for a pattern in many cases
explanations.definition: A pattern search measures the same thing in many people or things and looks for what goes together. The more cases you measure, the steadier the pattern.
explanations.description: Some questions cannot be answered by changing one thing. You cannot change how tall a person is to see what happens to their arms. So you measure many people and look. Are the taller people the ones with the longer arm spans? Draw the numbers in a table or on a graph and look for a pattern. One person tells you very little, because every person is a little different. Six or ten people tell you more, and a hundred tell you more again. Every measurement also wobbles a little, so a good pattern is one that stays visible through the wobble. A pattern tells you what goes together. It does not tell you what causes what.
examples: Measure the arm span and height of eight people and see whether the two numbers are close.
Count the petals on twenty flowers of the same kind and see whether the number is nearly always the same.
Note the time each school bus arrives on twenty mornings and look for the usual time and the wobble.
explanations.art: A table of eight people with two columns, height and arm span, next to a dotted graph with the dots lying close to a rising line.

explanations.concept: A pattern is not the same as a cause
explanations.definition: When two things go together, one may cause the other, or a third thing may cause both, or it may be chance. A pattern alone cannot tell you which.
explanations.description: Taller people have longer arms. Does being tall make your arms long? Partly, because the same growing body makes both. Something else goes along with height too: older children are taller, and they also have bigger shoes. Bigger shoes do not make children taller. Age makes both bigger. When we find a pattern, we should say 'these go together' and then ask why. To find out whether one thing causes another, we need a fair test, where we change one thing ourselves. If we cannot, we keep looking for other things that could explain the pattern.
examples: Shoe size and reading ability go together in primary school, because both grow with age.
Ice cream sales and sunburn cases go up together, because both happen on hot sunny days.
Tall people have long arms because one growing body makes both, not because one causes the other.
explanations.art: Three circles: age, shoe size and reading level, with arrows from age to the other two and none between shoe size and reading.

explanations.concept: When the result is a surprise
explanations.definition: A surprising result is a result that does not match your prediction. Check it, repeat it, write it down as it is, and then ask what it could mean.
explanations.description: Sometimes a test gives a result that nobody expected. The first thing to do is not to throw it away. First check that you did the test the way you planned, and read the measurement again. Then repeat the test. If the surprise happens again, it is real, and you have learned something new. It may mean the idea was wrong, or that a detail you did not think of matters. If it does not happen again, write down that the first result was probably a slip. Many important discoveries began as a surprising result that someone kept and looked at. Jocelyn Bell noticed a strange mark on a paper chart and would not let it go.
examples: You expect the warm tumbler to stay dry, but it gets a few drops. Perhaps the room is very humid.
One person's arm span is 10 centimetres more than their height. Measure again before you decide it is real.
A pigeon stays on the tank after the usual time. Write it down. It may be one pigeon, or a clue.
explanations.art: A hand holding a strange squiggle on a paper chart with a magnifying glass over it, and a note: check, repeat, write it down.

explanations.concept: Why we see what we expect
explanations.definition: People notice and remember what fits their idea more than what does not. Writing the prediction first, and asking what would show us wrong, helps us fight this habit.
explanations.description: When an idea feels right to us, we tend to notice the evidence for it and overlook the evidence against it. This happens to children and grown-ups, and to scientists too. A person who thinks the bell scares the pigeons will notice the evenings when the bell and the leaving happen together. They may not even notice the evening the bell was late. Psychologists have shown this in many experiments. The cure is not to stop having ideas. The cure is to write the predictions before the test, to ask 'what would show me wrong?' and to ask someone who disagrees to look at the results too.
examples: Two friends who each hope their team wins see the same close match and each count different fouls.
A child who expects the lemon slice to stay white may not look closely at a brown edge.
Francis Bacon, an English thinker, wrote in 1620 that a mind that has taken up an idea draws everything else in to support it.
explanations.art: Two people looking through different coloured glasses at the same drawing and seeing different things.

explanations.concept: Signal or noise? Jocelyn Bell's star-time test
explanations.definition: A signal is a pattern that carries information. Noise is random wobble. To check whether a strange mark is a signal from far away or noise from nearby, ask when it comes back.
explanations.description: In 1967 Jocelyn Bell was a research student at Cambridge in England. She was checking long paper charts from a radio telescope, a set of wires that listens for radio waves from space. She noticed a small strange mark, which she called a 'bit of scruff'. It came again. At first the team asked if it was interference from something on Earth, such as a car or a radio. Here was a deciding question. A thing in the sky rises and sets with the stars, and comes back about four minutes earlier by the clock each day. A car or a machine follows the clock on the wall. The mark followed the stars. So it came from space. We now know that it came from a pulsar.
examples: A noisy machine next door follows the clock. A star follows star time, about four minutes earlier each day.
A radio crackle every evening at six may be a neighbour's machine. A crackle that moves earlier each day may not be.
Astronomers still check strange signals by asking if they come back at star time.
explanations.art: A paper chart with a small repeating bump marked with an arrow, and a clock face beside a star map showing the bump coming four minutes earlier each day.

explanations.concept: How do pigeons tell that evening is coming?
explanations.definition: Many town birds settle for the night as the light fades, and a dark cloudy evening can send them to roost early. Scientists know that light matters. They are still working out exactly how birds judge it.
explanations.description: Birds have eyes, and they also have light-sensitive cells deep in the brain. Scientists have found that these help a bird tell day length and the time of year. Evening roosting seems to depend on how bright the sky is, and also on the bird's own inner body clock. Birds in cities also meet street lights, which can change when they sleep. We do not yet know exactly how all these signals are added up by the bird. This is a good example of an idea where we know a part and are still asking.
examples: Many crows gather to roost in the same trees around dusk in Indian cities.
Street lights can keep some city birds singing late into the night, which scientists have studied.
A very dark rain cloud in the afternoon can send birds to roost early.
explanations.art: Pigeons settling along a rooftop edge under an orange evening sky with a faint streetlight beginning to glow.

explanations.concept: Can every question be answered by a test?
explanations.description: Some questions can be answered by looking, counting or testing, such as how many drops formed in ten minutes. Other questions are about taste, kindness or what is fair. A test can tell us whether a cheaper medicine works. It cannot by itself tell us whether it is fair that some people cannot afford any. People disagree about where the line between testable questions and other questions falls.
examples: Which tumbler keeps water coldest? A test can answer it.
Which song is nicest? Each person's answer is true for them, so a test does not settle it.
Is it fair to test a new medicine on people? A test can tell us how it works. People must still argue about what is fair.
explanations.art: A signpost with two arms, one labelled can be tested and the other labelled needs arguing about, with example cards below each.

perspectives.explanation: Science answers only the questions that a test or an observation can settle. Questions about what is right, beautiful or fair belong to other kinds of thinking, and the two should not be mixed up.

Science and values meet all the time. What scientists choose to ask, which tests are allowed, and what we do with the results all depend on what people care about. Evidence helps us argue about fairness, even if it cannot settle it alone.

agreed.text: What we observe can be checked by others. What we infer is a guess until it has been tested.
agreed.evidence: When two people look at the same wet tumbler, they agree on the drops. They often disagree on where the water came from, until a test is done.

agreed.text: Drops on the outside of a cold tumbler come from water vapour in the air, which turns into liquid when it touches the cold wall.
agreed.evidence: Coloured water inside leaves the outside drops clear. A warm tumbler stays dry. A very cold glass left on a sensitive scale slowly gets heavier as drops collect.

agreed.text: When two explanations fit everything you have seen, you need a new observation where they disagree to choose between them.
agreed.evidence: This is how scientists have separated rival explanations for centuries. Francesco Redi, an Italian doctor, did it in 1668 by covering some jars of meat with cloth and leaving others open, to see whether maggots came from the meat itself or from flies.

agreed.text: An idea is useful to science only if some result could show it wrong.
agreed.evidence: Ideas that can fit every possible result cannot be checked by anyone, so they cannot be improved by testing.

agreed.text: A regular signal that returns at star time comes from far away, and not from machines on Earth.
agreed.evidence: Jocelyn Bell's team found that the pulses followed star time, and other radio telescopes found the same signals.

agreed.text: Arm span and height are close in most people, but not equal in everyone.
agreed.evidence: Measurements of many people show that arm span is usually within a few centimetres of height. Everyone's measurements also wobble a little.

challenging.claim: I saw the water leak through the steel.
challenging.for: Water appears on the outside of a cold tumbler. It is easy to think it came from the inside.
challenging.against: Nobody can see water crossing steel. What was seen was drops on the outside. A drop of coloured water inside leaves the outside drops clear, which shows the water came from somewhere else.

challenging.claim: If I watch carefully enough, the answer will appear on its own.
challenging.who: A common idea about how scientists work.
challenging.for: Careful watching helps us notice what is there, and many discoveries began with someone noticing something.
challenging.against: Watching gives us observations, not explanations. When two explanations fit the same observations, watching more of the same cannot choose. A good question can.

challenging.claim: There is one scientific method, with fixed steps that every scientist follows in the same order.
challenging.for: Questions, predictions, tests and conclusions do appear again and again in science, and a list of steps is easy to teach.
challenging.against: Real scientists mix their ways of working. Astronomers cannot change a star. Fossil hunters cannot repeat the past. Many discoveries began with a surprise, not a plan. The steps are a useful guide, but not a rule.

challenging.claim: One good test can prove an idea true for ever.
challenging.for: A clear result, repeated by many people, can make an idea very strong.
challenging.against: A test can show an idea wrong at once. It can only add to the case for an idea being right. A new test in a new place might still show a problem. This is why scientists say 'the evidence supports' more often than 'it is proved'.

challenging.claim: A surprising result means the test went wrong, so it can be thrown away.
challenging.who: Many students, and sometimes experienced people.
challenging.for: Sometimes a surprise really is a slip, such as a misread number.
challenging.against: Some surprises are the discovery. The only way to know is to check, repeat and keep the record. Rubbing out an odd result hides the very thing that might teach you something.

challenging.claim: If two things go together, one must cause the other.
challenging.for: Sometimes it is true. Fire and smoke go together, and fire causes smoke.
challenging.against: A third thing can cause both, as age makes feet and reading skill grow together. Or it can be chance. Only a fair test, or careful extra evidence, can tell which.

challenging.claim: Questions about what is fair or good are science questions, because science can answer everything.
challenging.for: Evidence can help us argue about fairness, for example by showing who is harmed by a rule.
challenging.against: A test shows what happens. It does not by itself say what we ought to do. People have to talk and decide about that, using evidence as one part of the talk.

big_questions.q: Everyone at the tumbler saw the same drops, yet people told different stories about them. Is the story part of what you see?
big_questions.hint: Try to describe the drops without using the word 'because'. How much is left?

big_questions.q: Is there anything you have ever seen without adding some idea to it?
big_questions.hint: Think about a face. When you see someone frowning, what did your eyes give you and what did you add?

big_questions.q: If two ideas fit all the evidence for a hundred years, do we have to choose one?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the two ideas would each predict about a new test nobody has done yet.

big_questions.q: The air in your room is full of water you cannot see. What else is around you that you cannot see?
big_questions.hint: Think about radio waves, smells and the air itself.

big_questions.q: Jocelyn Bell was a student when she noticed the strange mark, and a more senior person received the Nobel Prize. Who gets to ask the questions, and who gets the credit?
big_questions.hint: Think about who looked at the charts every day, and who was able to have their name on the prize.

big_questions.q: Why do people sometimes hold on to an explanation after a test has shown it wrong?
big_questions.hint: Think about how it feels to be wrong, and about who else shared the idea with you.

big_questions.q: Is there a question that no test could ever answer?
big_questions.hint: Think about 'What does a crow dream about?' and 'What happened before the Big Bang?' What would a test need?

big_questions.q: A fish darting in a pond looks happy to you. How could you find out whether she is?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you could observe, and what you can only infer.

big_questions.q: When we ask a question, we have already decided what to look at. What do we miss by asking this question and not another?
big_questions.hint: Think about the tumbler. If you only asked about the drops, would you have asked about the air?

big_questions.q: Do other animals ask questions? What would a crow's question look like?
big_questions.hint: Think about a crow dropping a nut on the road. What would they be finding out?

story.title: The Pigeons and the Bell
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real: many town birds settle for the night as the light fades, and a dark cloudy evening can send them to roost early. The flat, the bell, the pigeons' timings and the two weeks are imagined.
text: Chitra lived with her Ajji on the third floor of a flat in Mysuru. From their balcony you could see the water tank on the roof of the next building. Every evening, forty or fifty pigeons sat along the edge of the tank.
That November her cousin Kiran came to stay for two weeks. He was seven and he asked questions about everything. How many windows are there? Why does the lift hum? Where do the pigeons go?

On the first evening, the two of them stood on the balcony with glasses of warm milk. Across the road, the little temple began to ring its evening bell. At that very moment all the pigeons lifted off the tank together. They circled once and flew away over the roofs.
"The bell scared them," said Kiran. "I saw it."
Ajji was in the kitchen, but she had good ears. "What did you see," she called, "and what did you add?"
This was Ajji's rule. Whenever somebody said "because" in her house, she asked the same thing. Chitra grinned. She knew what to do.
"You saw the bell ring," she told Kiran. "You saw the pigeons fly. You did not see the bell scare them. The scaring is the part you added."
Kiran thought about this with his milk moustache. "Then what is your idea?"
"Pigeons go to sleep at dusk," said Chitra. "Maybe they leave because the light is going." She opened her notebook and wrote two ideas, one under the other. The bell. The dusk.
"It is the bell," said Kiran. "The bell is loud."
Ajji came out, wiping her hands. "Two ideas," she said. "Good. Now, if the first one is true, what else will you see? And if the second is true, what else?"
Chitra chewed her pencil. Then she wrote carefully. If the bell scares them, they will leave when the bell rings. If the dusk sends them, they will leave when the light goes.
She stopped. "But the bell rings at six, and the light goes at about six. The two ideas say exactly the same thing!"
"Aha," said Kiran. "So I win?"
"No. Nobody wins." Chitra was thinking fast now. "We could watch every evening for a year. Every evening would fit both ideas. Watching more of the same cannot choose between them."
"So what can?" asked Ajji, in her quiet teacher voice.
"An evening when the two ideas disagree," said Chitra. "One where the light goes at a different time from the bell."
"We cannot make the bell ring at a different time," said Kiran. "The priest will not listen to me."
Chitra looked up at the sky. The grey November clouds were already piling up in the west. "Maybe the sky will do it for us."

For three evenings they watched and wrote. Day, bell, pigeons, sky. The pigeons left just as the bell began, and the sky was bright until the very end. On the fourth evening, black rain clouds rolled in before half past four. By five the streetlights were on, and the balcony was dim.
They stood at the door with the notebook and a pencil. Kiran held his breath. At twelve minutes past five, the pigeons lifted off the tank, circled and left. The bell had not rung.
"They went early," whispered Kiran. They waited. At six the bell rang. The tank was empty and nothing moved.
"So it is not the bell," said Kiran, a little sadly.
"Not on this evening," said Chitra. "But you have a good point coming, I can see it."
Kiran jumped. "What if the rain scared them? Rain is loud, too!"
Chitra beamed. "A third idea. Good. Now we need a dark evening with no rain." She wrote it down.

Two evenings later the sky was thick and grey all afternoon, but no drop fell. The pigeons left early again, when the light had gone dim. And one more evening, the temple priest was away and the bell did not ring at all. The pigeons left at the usual time.
Ajji read the notebook for a long time. "So, what can you say?"

Chitra wrote slowly. "On the evenings we watched, the pigeons left when the light went. They did not leave when the bell rang. We watched one tank for two weeks. We cannot say this is true for every pigeon in Mysuru."
"Good," said Ajji. "You said what your evidence says and not one word more."
Kiran was frowning at the empty tank. "But how do the pigeons know the light is going? They do not have clocks."
Chitra shrugged. "I do not know. That is the next question."
Kiran took the notebook, turned to a fresh page and wrote the question at the top. Under it he wrote, in large letters, "Idea one." Then he left a lot of space.
story.epiphany: When two ideas both fit what you have seen, watching more of the same cannot choose between them. You need a day when the ideas predict different things. Then the day itself gives the answer.
ask: Why could Chitra not choose between the bell and the dusk after the first few evenings?
What was the deciding question that Chitra found, and what did each idea predict about it?
Kiran suggested a third idea, that the rain scared the pigeons. How did Chitra test it?
Chitra said she could not be sure about every pigeon in Mysuru. Why was that a good thing to say?
What is the next question that Kiran asked, and how might you find out?

games.context: This is a card game about two kinds of sentences. One kind says what you noticed. The other kind says what you think it means. You sort 24 sentences into the right kind.

setup.art: Twenty-four sentence cards in a shuffled pile with two kinds of tokens in front of each player, one saying I SAW and one saying I THINK.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: one sentence on the front, and the answer with the reason on the back

items.f: The milk in the pan has a skin on top.
items.b: I SAW. You can look at the pan and see the skin. Anyone can check it.

items.f: The milk has gone off.
items.b: I THINK. It may be true, but you would need to smell it or check how long it sat out. 'Gone off' is a guess made from what you saw.

items.f: A crow is sitting on the balcony railing.
items.b: I SAW. You can see where the crow is.

items.f: The crow is waiting for food.
items.b: I THINK. Nobody saw what the crow wanted. The crow may be resting, or watching the street.

items.f: The steel katori feels colder than the wooden spoon.
items.b: I SAW, or more exactly, I FELT. It is what your hand reports, and anyone can check it by touching both.

items.f: The steel katori is colder than the wooden spoon.
items.b: I THINK. In the same room both have the same temperature. Steel only feels colder because it carries heat away from your hand faster.

items.f: The Sun moves across the sky from morning to evening.
items.b: I SAW. You can watch it go from one side of the sky to the other.

items.f: The Sun goes round the Earth.
items.b: I THINK. It is a story that fits what we see. Careful tests show that the Earth is turning, and that is why the Sun seems to move.

items.f: There are 14 ants on the sugar crumb.
items.b: I SAW. You can count them, and someone else can count too.

items.f: The ants smelled the sugar from far away.
items.b: I THINK. Nobody saw the smell travel. It is a good guess, and you could test it with a deciding question.

items.f: The money plant on the window is leaning towards the glass.
items.b: I SAW. You can look at the plant and see the lean.

items.f: The plant wants the sunlight.
items.b: I THINK. The lean is what we saw. 'Wants' is a guess about why. Plants do bend towards light, and a test with a lamp can show it.

items.f: My friend did not answer my message.
items.b: I SAW. There is no reply on the screen.

items.f: My friend is ignoring me.
items.b: I THINK. There are many other stories, such as a flat battery, a busy day or a missed message. You would need to ask.

items.f: The tap drips 30 times in one minute.
items.b: I SAW. You counted drips and watched the clock.

items.f: The washer inside the tap is worn.
items.b: I THINK. It could be, but nobody has looked inside. A plumber could check.

items.f: Little drops cover the outside of the cold bottle.
items.b: I SAW. They are there for anyone to see.

items.f: The bottle is leaking.
items.b: I THINK. It is a story about where the drops came from. A test with coloured water could check it.

items.f: The moong sprouts are 2 centimetres long.
items.b: I SAW. You measured them with a ruler.

items.f: The moong sprouts grew because I sang to them.
items.b: I THINK. Other stories fit too, such as the warmth, the water or the seeds themselves. You would need a fair test.

items.f: The bus came at 7:40, then 7:48, then 7:41.
items.b: I SAW. You wrote the times down on three mornings.

items.f: The bus driver is lazy on Tuesdays.
items.b: I THINK. The times are the evidence. 'Lazy' is a story added to them. Traffic or a different route may explain it.

items.f: The kolam at the door is smudged.
items.b: I SAW. You can look at the smudge.

items.f: Somebody stepped on the kolam.
items.b: I THINK. Wind, rain or a passing cat may also have smudged the kolam. Footprints or a small camera would settle it.

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. 2. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. 3. Give each player one I SAW token and one I THINK token.
flow.say: Some sentences say what you noticed. Some say what you think it means. In this game you sort them. Every player gets two tokens.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take two tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of the game Saw It or Thought It. You set up the cards and the tokens.
flow.parent: Cut the backs and fronts so each card has its answer on the reverse. If you cannot print, write the sentences on paper strips and keep the answers in a list.

flow.do: Read the first three cards as practice. Let everyone choose a token first. Then read the back of each card.
flow.say: Here is the first card. Do you think I SAW or I THINK? Hold up your token. Now we turn it over together. What does the back say?
flow.kid: Read a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.
flow.context: In this step, you play three practice cards and learn how to score.

check.q: A friend says, 'The dog is angry.' Is this I SAW or I THINK?
options: I SAW, because the dog is barking
I THINK, because nobody saw the dog's feelings
Neither
check.why: Anger is a story about why the dog barks. What you saw is the barking. A dog who barks at a gate may be scared, happy or guarding. We have to look for more evidence.

flow.do: Play the other 21 cards. Take turns being the reader. After each I THINK card, ask for a different story that fits.
flow.say: Read the front aloud. Everyone picks a token. Turn them over together. If the card was I THINK, who has another story that fits?
flow.kid: Take turns. Read a card, pick a token, check the back. For I THINK cards, say another story.
flow.context: In this step, you play most of the cards. You also practise making rival stories.

ask.q: A card says 'The ants smelled the sugar from far away.' What else might explain it?
good: They followed a trail left by another ant.
They saw the sugar.
They bumped into it by chance.

flow.parent: The best bonus points come from a story that is different from the first one and could be tested. 'Maybe not' is not a story. 'They followed a trail' is.

flow.do: Add up the points. Look at the cards that fooled you. Talk about what made them sound like 'I SAW' when they were 'I THINK'.
flow.say: Let's count the points. Which cards fooled someone? What made them sound like something we saw?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which card fooled you? Why?
flow.context: In this step, you add up and talk about the cards that tricked you.
flow.think: Words like because, wants, made and is angry are clues that a story slipped in. Can you spot more of them?

games.title: Tell Them Apart: pick the question that decides
games.context: This is a card game about rival explanations. Each card gives a puzzle with two ideas and three checks. You pick the check that can tell the ideas apart. The cards are thinking puzzles, so you do not need to run the checks. You may try the safe ones at home, with a grown-up.

printables.title: 16 two-sided puzzle cards: a puzzle with two ideas and three checks on the front, and the answer on the back

items.f: A steel tumbler of cold water is wet on the outside. Idea A: the water leaked through the steel. Idea B: the water came out of the air. Which check tells them apart? 1) Put red colour in the water inside and look at the colour of the drops. 2) Look at the tumbler for longer. 3) Ask three friends which idea they like.
items.b: Check 1. If A is true, the drops will be red. If B is true, the drops will be clear. The other two checks cannot separate the ideas.

items.f: Pigeons leave the water tank every evening around six. Idea A: the temple bell scares them. Idea B: the fading light sends them. Which check tells them apart? 1) Watch ten more evenings like the last ones. 2) Watch an evening when the bell does not ring. 3) Count the pigeons each day.
items.b: Check 2. If A is true, the pigeons will stay on the bell-free evening. If B is true, they will leave anyway when the light fades. Check 1 gives the same results for both ideas.

items.f: A money plant on the windowsill leans towards the glass. Idea A: the plant leans towards the light. Idea B: the plant leans towards the fresh air from outside. Which check tells them apart? 1) Shut the window and put a lamp on the other side of the plant. 2) Water the plant more. 3) Measure how tall it is.
items.b: Check 1. If A is true, the plant will lean towards the lamp. If B is true, it will still lean towards the window. Watering and measuring do not separate the ideas.

items.f: Wet footprints lead from the bathroom to the kitchen. Idea A: Amma made them. Idea B: Appa made them. Which check tells them apart? 1) Mop the floor. 2) Measure the footprint and compare it with each person's foot. 3) Wait for them to dry.
items.b: Check 2. Each person's foot makes a different size of print. Mopping and waiting would destroy the evidence and not help to decide.

items.f: The curd set faster on a hot day. Idea A: the warmth did it. Idea B: the starter was fresher that day. Which check tells them apart? 1) Set two bowls of milk with the same starter, one in a warm place and one in a cool place. 2) Taste the curd. 3) Ask Ajji what she thinks.
items.b: Check 1. The starter is the same in both bowls, so only the warmth is different. If A is true, the warm bowl sets first. If B is true, the two bowls will set about together.

items.f: A steel spoon and a wooden spoon lie on the table. The steel feels colder. Idea A: the steel really is colder. Idea B: the steel only feels colder because it takes heat from your hand faster. Which check tells them apart? 1) Touch them again. 2) Leave them in the same room for an hour, and then put a room thermometer against each. 3) Weigh them.
items.b: Check 2. If A is true, the thermometer will read lower for the steel. If B is true, both will read the same. Touching again just repeats the feeling, and weighing does nothing to temperature.

items.f: A streetlight comes on at 6:10 pm. Idea A: a timer switches it at the same clock time each day. Idea B: a light sensor switches it when it gets dark. Which check tells them apart? 1) Watch it on a very dark, cloudy evening. 2) Look closely at the bulb. 3) Count the poles on the street.
items.b: Check 1. A timer switches the light at the same time on the cloudy evening. A sensor switches it earlier, because it is darker. Looking at the bulb tells you nothing about what switches it.

items.f: A line of ants goes to a sugar crumb. Idea A: they follow a smell trail left by the ants before them. Idea B: each ant finds the sugar on their own. Which check tells them apart? 1) Wipe a short piece of the ants' path with a damp cloth and watch what they do. 2) Count the ants. 3) Give them a bigger crumb.
items.b: Check 1. If A is true, ants will get confused at the wiped patch, because the trail is gone. If B is true, they will carry straight on. Counting or giving a bigger crumb does not separate the ideas. Wipe only the path and never touch the ants, because some bite.

items.f: Cloudy water from the tap clears in a minute. Idea A: it is full of tiny air bubbles. Idea B: it is full of tiny bits of mud. Which check tells them apart? 1) Let a glass stand and see whether it clears from the bottom or from the top. 2) Taste it. 3) Shake the glass.
items.b: Check 1. Air bubbles rise, so the water clears from the bottom first. Mud sinks, so the water clears from the top first. Never taste water to decide, because it may not be safe.

items.f: Washing dries faster outside. Idea A: the Sun's warmth does it. Idea B: the breeze does it. Which check tells them apart? 1) Dry one cloth in sunshine behind a closed glass window, and one in the shade with a fan on it. 2) Hang it higher. 3) Use a bigger cloth.
items.b: Check 1. The first cloth gets warmth but no breeze. The second gets a breeze but no direct sun. Whichever dries first shows which idea matters more. Hanging it higher or using a bigger cloth changes other things and does not separate the ideas.

items.f: Moong seeds in a pot on the window sprouted before moong seeds in a cupboard. Idea A: light helps seeds sprout. Idea B: the window was warmer. Which check tells them apart? 1) Keep both pots in the same warm place, one in the light and one in the dark. 2) Give the cupboard seeds more water. 3) Wait another week.
items.b: Check 1. Now the warmth is the same, so any difference comes from the light. Giving more water or waiting leaves the two ideas still mixed up. Note that many seeds sprout well in the dark, so your result might surprise you.

items.f: A new pen writes more smoothly than an old pen. Idea A: the new pen is better. Idea B: the paper you wrote on was smoother. Which check tells them apart? 1) Write with both pens on the same sheet of paper. 2) Press harder with the old one. 3) Ask a friend.
items.b: Check 1. The paper is the same for both, so the pen is the only difference. If A is true, the new pen still writes more smoothly. If B is true, the two pens will feel alike.

items.f: A humming sound comes from the kitchen wall at night. Idea A: the fridge is making it. Idea B: the water pipes are making it. Which check tells them apart? 1) Ask a grown-up to switch the fridge off for two minutes and listen. 2) Put a pillow on your head. 3) Wait until morning.
items.b: Check 1. If A is true, the hum stops when the fridge is off, and the grown-up should switch it back on afterwards. If B is true, the hum carries on. A pillow or waiting does not tell the ideas apart.

items.f: The kolam at the door is gone by the evening. Idea A: people walking over it rub it away. Idea B: the wind blows it away. Which check tells them apart? 1) Draw one small kolam indoors where people walk but there is no wind, and one on a quiet balcony ledge where the wind blows but nobody walks. 2) Draw it bigger. 3) Draw it earlier in the morning.
items.b: Check 1. If A is true, the indoor kolam will fade and the balcony kolam will stay. If B is true, it will be the other way round. Drawing it bigger or earlier changes neither idea.

items.f: The wooden door sticks in the monsoon but not in summer. Idea A: the wood swells in the damp. Idea B: the hinges rust. Which check tells them apart? 1) Put a few drops of oil on the hinges and see whether the door still sticks on a damp day. 2) Push harder. 3) Paint the door.
items.b: Check 1. If B is true, oiling the hinges frees the door. If A is true, the door still sticks. Pushing harder or painting does not separate the ideas.

items.f: The Moon looks bigger when it is low over the roofs than when it is high in the sky. Idea A: it really is closer when low. Idea B: it is a trick of our eyes and the sizes are the same. Which check tells them apart? 1) Hold a grain of rice at arm's length and see how much of the Moon it covers when the Moon is low and again when it is high. 2) Look at it through a tube. 3) Ask someone taller.
items.b: Check 1. If A is true, the grain will cover less of the low Moon than of the high Moon. If B is true, it will cover the same amount both times. People who try this find the sizes match, so our eyes are tricked.

experiments.title: The Weeping Tumbler: where do the drops come from?
experiments.question: A steel tumbler of ice water gets wet on the outside. Did the water leak through the steel, or did it come from the air?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. What will happen to the outside of a tumbler filled with ice water? Where do you think the water will come from? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: This test puts two ideas against each other. It does not change one thing to see what it does. The deciding question is the colour of the drops. Leaking predicts coloured drops, and water from the air predicts clear drops. To keep it fair, both tumblers are the same size and start dry. They stand on the same kind of plate in the same place and are checked at the same times. The warm tumbler is the control, because it shows what the room does when the steel is not cold.
results_table: Cold tumbler: what the outside looks like
Cold tumbler: colour of the drops
Warm tumbler: what the outside looks like

materials.item: 2 tumblers of the same size and material. Clear glass is best, because you can see the coloured water inside. Steel works too, but you cannot see the colour through it, so peek in from above
6 to 8 ice cubes and some chilled water from the fridge
warm tap water, comfortable to touch but not hot
food colour (red or blue) or a pinch of haldi, enough to colour the water strongly
2 dry plates or saucers
dry tissues or a clean dry cloth
a phone timer, a pencil and a notebook

experiments.safety: Use warm tap water, never hot water from a kettle. A grown-up should pour for young children, and handle glass tumblers, since glass can break. Food colour and haldi stain clothes, so work on a tray or a table you can wipe.
experiments.record: Fill in the results table at 5, 10 and 15 minutes. Write the minute you first saw drops on the cold tumbler. Draw both tumblers at 15 minutes, and colour in the water inside and the drops outside.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you see drops form on the outside of a cold tumbler and you test two rival ideas about where they come from.

setup.caption: 3. Wait and watch. Look at 5, 10 and 15 minutes.

flow.say: We will fill this tumbler with ice water. In ten minutes, what do you think the outside will look like? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A tumbler of ice water. What will the outside look like in ten minutes? Why?
