ask.q: What do you think will happen on the outside? Why?
good: It will get wet, because the ice makes it sweat.
Nothing, because the steel is shut.
It will get wet, because the water leaks through.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write exactly what your child says. Any guess with a reason is a good start.

flow.do: Tell your child that people disagree about where the water comes from. Write two ideas. Idea A: the water leaked through the steel. Idea B: the water came from the air. Ask for a third idea. Then ask for an if-then sentence for each idea about the colour of the drops.
flow.say: Some people say the water leaks through the steel. Some say it comes from the air. Do you have another idea? If we colour the water inside red, what will we see outside if idea A is true? And if idea B is true?
flow.kid: Two ideas. A: it leaks through. B: it comes from the air. What colour will the drops be for each?
flow.context: In this step, you write the rival ideas and what each one predicts, before any test.

ask.q: If the water leaked through, what colour would the drops be?
good: Red, like the water inside.
The same colour as the water inside.

ask.q: If the water came from the air, what colour would the drops be?
good: Clear.
No colour, because the air has no colour.

flow.parent: If your child says 'sweat from my hands' or 'from the ice', write it down as Idea C. A good deciding question for Idea C is: do the drops also appear when no hand has touched the tumbler? The coloured water in the next step will help with that too.

check.q: Why do we write the if-then sentences before the test?
options: So we cannot say afterwards that we expected the result
So the test is faster
So the tumblers stay cold
check.why: A written prediction is fixed. If we only decide afterwards, it is easy to believe we expected the result all along. Writing first keeps the test honest.

flow.do: 1. Fill the first tumbler three-quarters with chilled water. Add 6 to 8 ice cubes. Stir in the colour until the water is strongly coloured. 2. Fill the second tumbler with warm tap water and the same amount of colour. 3. Wipe the outside of both tumblers completely dry. Do not touch the outsides again. 4. Put each tumbler on its own dry plate. 5. Start the timer and write the time.
flow.say: Fill this one with chilled water and ice. Fill the other with warm water. Add the same colour to both. Now dry the outsides well. Do not touch them again.
flow.kid: Fill one tumbler with ice water. Fill one with warm water. Add colour. Dry the outsides.
flow.context: In this step, you set up both tumblers so they start dry and the same, except for the temperature.
flow.parent: Wipe up every drop of colour from the outside when you pour. If colour is on the outside, the drops there will look coloured and spoil the test. Use warm tap water, not hot. Stand the plates side by side so the room is the same for both.

flow.do: At 5, 10 and 15 minutes, look at both tumblers. Write what the outside looks like. Then lift a drop from the cold tumbler on a dry tissue and look at its colour. Draw the cold tumbler at 15 minutes.
flow.say: Look at the cold tumbler. What do you see on the outside? Touch a dry tissue to a drop. What colour is it? Now look at the warm tumbler. What is different?
flow.kid: Look at both tumblers at 5, 10 and 15 minutes. What colour are the drops?
flow.context: In this step, you watch for drops and check their colour.
flow.parent: Roles for 2 to 4 children: one watches the cold tumbler, one watches the warm tumbler, one keeps the timer and one writes the table. Swap roles at each look. With one child, you take the timer and the writing. Hold the tissue to a drop and look at the damp spot it leaves. A red spot means colour, and a spot with no colour means a clear drop. In a humid kitchen, the cold tumbler is usually covered in fine drops within 5 to 10 minutes. On a dry day, or in an air-conditioned room, it can take 15 to 20 minutes. If there are no drops after 15 minutes, add more ice and wait 10 more minutes. You can also breathe gently onto the cold steel. Your breath is full of water vapour, so mist forms at once. The warm tumbler should stay dry or show only a very faint mist at the start. Drops that look slightly pink mean there was a little colour on the outside. Wipe it and look again.

check.q: The water inside is red. The drops on the outside are clear. What does this show?
options: The drops did not come from the water inside
The tumbler leaked a little
The colour was too weak
check.why: If the red water had crossed the steel, the drops would be red. They are clear, so they came from somewhere else. This is evidence against the leaking idea.

flow.wait: Wait 5 minutes between looks. Read the explanation card 'Rival explanations' while you wait.

flow.do: 1. On the cold tumbler, wipe one patch of the outside dry with a tissue. 2. Watch that patch for three minutes. 3. Ask your child where the new drops come from, if there is no hole.
flow.say: I will wipe this patch dry. Watch it for three minutes. What do you notice? If the steel leaked, where would the water come from now?
flow.kid: Wipe one patch dry. Watch it. Do new drops come back?
flow.context: In this step, you use a second test. You wipe one patch dry and see if drops return.

ask.q: Where do the new drops on the dry patch come from?
good: From the air.
From the air touching the cold steel.
Not from inside, because the steel is shut.

flow.parent: The wiped patch fogs over again within a few minutes. A leaking tumbler would need tiny holes, and the drops would reappear only at those spots. Here the drops appear everywhere on the cold wall, and also low down on the plate edge. This supports the air idea.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write a claim, the evidence and the reasoning. Then read the explanation 'Why drops form on the outside of a cold tumbler'.
flow.say: What do you think happened? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened that way?
flow.kid: What did you find? What did you see? Why do you think so?
flow.context: In this step, you say what you found, what you saw and why. Then you read the science.

ask.q: What do you think, what did you see, and why?
good: The water came from the air. The drops were clear but the water inside was red. The air has water vapour that turns to drops on the cold steel.
I was wrong. I thought it leaked, but the colour stayed inside.

ask.q: Was your first guess right? Does it matter if it was wrong?
good: It does not matter. The test shows what happens.
I was surprised, and that is useful.

flow.parent: Say well done for any honest result. If the drops were coloured, look for colour on the outside from pouring, or for a crack in the tumbler. Repeat with a clean tumbler.

check.q: The warm tumbler stayed dry. What does this tell us about the drops on the cold one?
options: The cold steel matters, because the same air did not make drops on the warm one
The warm tumbler was too small
The ice made the drops by melting
check.why: The air and the room were the same for both tumblers. Only the steel temperature was different. So the cold steel is what made the drops form.

experiments.title: Arm Span and Height: is Leonardo right?
experiments.question: Is a person's arm span (finger tip to finger tip, arms stretched out) the same as their height? Is the pattern the same for children and grown-ups?
experiments.predict: Before you measure, guess. Will your arm span be shorter than your height, the same, or longer? Will it be the same for a grown-up? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: This is a pattern search, not a fair test, because we cannot change a person's height to see what happens. We keep the measuring fair in other ways. Everyone is measured in bare feet, standing straight against the same wall. The same helper reads the tape, and we measure to the nearest centimetre. We write down every person we measure and we leave nobody out because the number looks odd.

materials.item: a measuring tape of at least 2 metres (a 150 cm sewing tape is too short for most grown-ups), or a long string and a ruler or metre stick
a wall with a clear floor beside it, and 3 sticky notes or small pieces of masking tape (pencil marks may not rub off a painted wall)
a flat book or tray for marking the top of the head
a pencil and a notebook
6 or more people to measure, such as family, neighbours or friends

experiments.safety: Ask each person before you measure them. Do not stand on chairs to reach the top of the wall.
experiments.record: Fill in the results table for each person. Draw a number line from minus 10 to plus 10 and put a dot for each person's span minus height.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you measure the height and arm span of six or more people and look for a pattern, as Leonardo da Vinci drew about 1490.

setup.art: A girl standing barefoot with her back against a wall while a helper holds a flat book on her head and marks the wall with a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Measure height. Stand against the wall. A helper marks the top of the head.

setup.art: A girl standing against a wall with her arms stretched out wide like a letter T, and a helper placing a sticky note at each middle fingertip.
setup.caption: 2. Measure arm span. Stretch your arms wide and mark each middle fingertip.

setup.art: A helper pulling a tape measure straight between two sticky notes on a wall.
setup.caption: 3. Measure the distance between the marks.

setup.art: A table in a notebook with six rows of people and four columns of numbers.
setup.caption: 4. Write each person in the table. Work out span minus height.

setup.art: A number line from minus 10 to plus 10 with dots of different colours placed along it.
setup.caption: 5. Put a dot on the number line for each person.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess whether arm span will be shorter than height, the same, or longer. Ask why. Write the guess. Draw the results table.
flow.say: Stretch your arms out wide. Do you think the distance from fingertip to fingertip is shorter than your height, the same or longer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Arms wide. Is your span shorter, the same, or longer than your height? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Arm Span test. You guess before you measure.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Arms are long, so the span is longer.
My arms are shorter than my body, so the span is shorter.
They look about the same.

flow.parent: Write the guess and reason at the top. Do not say what Leonardo drew yet.

flow.do: 1. Take off shoes. 2. Stand with the back of the head, shoulders and heels against the wall, looking straight ahead. 3. A helper lays a flat book on the head, level against the wall. The helper sticks a sticky note just under the book. 4. Measure from the floor to the mark. 5. Do this twice, and write both numbers.
flow.say: Stand tall with your back against the wall. Look straight ahead. Now I will mark the top of your head. We will measure twice. Do you think we will get the same number?
flow.kid: Stand against the wall. Your helper marks the top of your head. Measure twice.
flow.context: In this step, you practise measuring height and see that two measurements of the same child may differ a little.

ask.q: The two heights were not exactly the same. Why might that happen?
good: The tape was not straight.
I stood a little differently.
We read the tape in a different place.

flow.parent: A difference of 1 or 2 centimetres between measurements is normal, because the head moves and the tape bends. Do not worry about it. Say that this wobble is why we measure several people.

check.q: You measure the same child twice and get 128 cm and 129 cm. What is the best thing to do?
options: Write both numbers and use the bigger one or the middle, and say there is about a centimetre of wobble
Throw away one and not say
Measure a third time and hide the other two
check.why: Every measurement wobbles a little. Writing both numbers is honest. A small difference like this is normal measurement error, not a mistake.

flow.do: 1. Stand with your back flat against the wall and your arms stretched out wide, like a letter T. 2. A helper puts a sticky note at the tip of each middle finger. 3. Step away. 4. Pull the tape straight and measure from one note to the other. 5. Measure twice and write both numbers.
flow.say: Back against the wall. Arms out wide like a T. Hold still. I will put a sticky note at each fingertip. Then we measure between them.
flow.kid: Back to the wall. Arms out like a T. Your helper marks your fingertips.
flow.context: In this step, you measure your own arm span.
flow.parent: The wall must be wider than the arm span. If it is not, stand in a corner with one fingertip touching the corner and mark the other on the wall. Keep the tape level, not sagging.

flow.do: Measure the other people the same way. Write each person's name or initial, their height and their arm span in the table. Subtract height from span to fill the last column. A negative number means span is shorter than height.
flow.say: Now we measure everyone else the same way. Write each number in the table. Then take away the height from the span. If the span is shorter, the answer is a number below zero.
flow.kid: Measure at least five more people. Write each person in your table.
flow.context: In this step, you measure at least five more people and fill in the table.
flow.parent: Roles for 2 to 4 children: one stands, one holds the book and the sticky note, one holds the tape, one writes. Swap so each child measures and is measured. With one child, you are the helper and measure the child, then yourself with your child's help. You need at least six people. If your home has only four, ask two neighbours or friends. You can also measure again on another day. Measure at least one child and at least one grown-up. Children grow, so their spans may differ from adults' spans in a different way.

flow.do: 1. Look at the last column. Count how many people are within 3 centimetres of zero. 2. Find the person farthest from zero. 3. Put the dots on a number line. 4. Look at the children and grown-ups separately.
flow.say: Look at the last column. How many people have a difference close to zero? Who is farthest? Do the children look different from the grown-ups?
flow.kid: Count how many people are close to zero. Who is the farthest? What do you notice?
flow.context: In this step, you look for the pattern in your numbers.

ask.q: What pattern do you see?
good: Most people have a span close to their height.
The span is a little longer for the grown-ups.
One person is far from the rest.

ask.q: What would you do about the person who is far from the rest?
good: Measure them again.
Check the tape was straight.
Write them in anyway if it is the same twice.

flow.do: Ask your child to say a claim, the evidence and the reason. Then ask what the numbers cannot tell us. Read the explanation 'Looking for a pattern in many cases'.
flow.say: What can you say about span and height from your numbers? What can you not say?
flow.kid: What did you find? What can't you say from only a few people?
flow.context: In this step, you write a careful conclusion from your numbers. You also say what you cannot tell.

ask.q: What can't we say from only a few people?
good: That it is true for everyone in the world.
That it is true for babies or for very old people.
That one thing causes the other.

flow.parent: A typical result is that most people are within a few centimetres of zero, with some a little over and some under. Grown-ups, especially men, often have a span a few centimetres longer than their height, and the numbers wobble more with a small group, so do not be surprised if only half your people are within 3 centimetres. Leonardo drew arm span equal to height, but real people vary. If your child's numbers are all over the place, check the measuring before you decide there is no pattern.

check.q: Six people have an arm span within 4 centimetres of their height. Which claim goes too far?
options: Everybody in the world has an arm span exactly equal to their height
In the people we measured, arm span was close to height
Arm span and height tend to go together
check.why: Our six people can only show what happens for those six. 'Close' is not 'exactly'. And we cannot speak for everybody from a small sample.

activities.title: The Kitchen Scene: what I saw, what I think

materials.item: a plate with a few crumbs and a banana peel
a half-full glass of water with a wet ring on the table beneath it
a chair pulled out from the table and one slipper lying on its side
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Keep it a quiet scene. Do not leave water where someone can slip. Use an old peel and crumbs that nobody will eat, so food allergies do not matter.

schedule.what: Stage the scene. Write what you saw and what you think. Make a rival story and a deciding question.

activities.record: A page with two columns, I saw and I think. Under it, one rival story and one deciding question.
activities.context: In this activity, you stage a small scene in the kitchen and sort your sentences about it into what you saw and what you think.

setup.art: A kitchen table with a plate of crumbs, a banana peel, a half-full glass with a wet ring, a chair pulled out and a slipper on its side.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up stages a small scene on the kitchen table while you wait outside.

setup.art: A child writing in a notebook with two columns headed I saw and I think.
setup.caption: 2. Walk in. Write what you saw in one column and what you think in the other.

setup.art: A child drawing an arrow from a banana peel to two different small story pictures.
setup.caption: 3. Pick one story. Write a rival story and a way to tell them apart.

flow.do: While your child waits outside, stage the scene. Put crumbs and a banana peel on a plate. Add a half-full glass with a wet ring, a chair pulled out and a slipper on its side. Then call your child in.
flow.say: Close your eyes. I am setting a scene. Now come in and look carefully. Do not touch anything. What do you see?
flow.kid: Wait outside. A grown-up sets a scene. Then come in and look. Do not touch.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Kitchen Scene. A grown-up sets the scene.
flow.parent: Keep the scene gentle and silly. Avoid anything that looks like a real mess or a real accident.

flow.do: Ask your child to write six things they saw and three things they think happened. Draw two columns. Help them move any sentence with 'because' or 'must have' into the I think column.
flow.say: Write six things you can see. Then write three things you think happened. A sentence with 'because' or 'must have' goes in the second column.
flow.kid: Write six things you see. Write three things you think happened.
flow.context: In this step, you sort what you saw from what you think.

ask.q: How can you tell a sentence is in the wrong column?
good: It has because in it.
Someone else might say something different.
I did not see it, I worked it out.

check.q: Which sentence belongs in the 'I saw' column?
options: The banana peel is on the plate
Someone ate a banana here
Someone was in a hurry
check.why: The peel is there for anyone to see. 'Someone ate a banana here' and 'someone was in a hurry' are stories about what happened. They might be right, but nobody saw them.

flow.do: Ask your child to choose their favourite story. Then ask them to make one rival story that fits the same facts. Then ask: what could we check to tell the stories apart?
flow.say: Pick your favourite story. Now make a different story that fits the same facts. What could we check to tell them apart?
flow.kid: Pick one story. Make a rival story. How could you tell them apart?
flow.context: In this step, you make a rival story and a deciding question.

ask.q: What could you check to tell the stories apart?
good: Whether the peel is still wet or fresh.
Whether the glass is still cold.
Ask who was here.

flow.parent: Good deciding questions often use time: is the water ring still wet? Is the peel brown? Let your child swap places next. Your child stages a scene for you, and you write the columns. With 2 to 4 children, one stages the scene while the rest wait outside. Everyone writes their own two columns, then compares: whose I saw lists match, and whose I think stories differ?

activities.title: Message or Noise? Listening for a signal

materials.item: a steel plate or a table to tap on, and a spoon
a helper to tap, in another room or behind a door
a paper and a pencil
a fan or a radio to make background noise

schedule.what: Listen to two sets of taps. Decide if there is a signal. Add noise and try again.

activities.record: Draw a line of dots for each set of taps you heard, using short and long gaps. Write 'signal' or 'noise' under each. Write how many of the 12 taps you heard with the fan on low, medium and high.
activities.context: In this activity, you listen to taps from another room. You decide which set has a message and how you could be sure.

setup.art: A helper behind a door tapping a steel plate with a spoon while a child listens and draws dots on paper.
setup.caption: 1. A helper taps on a plate behind a door. You draw a dot for every tap.

setup.art: A row of dots drawn on a page with even gaps, next to a row with uneven gaps.
setup.caption: 2. Look at your dots. Are the gaps even or uneven?

setup.art: A fan running next to the helper while the child listens and draws.
setup.caption: 3. Add background noise and listen again.

flow.do: Ask your helper to go behind a door. Ask them to tap the plate 12 times in an uneven rhythm. Your child draws a dot for each tap and leaves a longer space for a longer gap.
flow.say: Listen carefully. Draw a dot every time you hear a tap. If the gap is long, leave a long space.
flow.kid: Listen to the taps. Draw a dot for each one.
flow.context: This is the first step of Message or Noise. You listen to uneven taps.
flow.parent: The helper should tap randomly, with no rhythm. Let your child know that there may or may not be a message. With 2 to 4 children, one is the tapper behind the door and the others listen and draw on their own papers. Swap roles after each set, then compare dots. With one child, you tap. Tap gently so the plate does not slip or ring loudly in the next room.

flow.do: Ask the helper to tap 12 times with an even gap of one second. Your child draws the dots again. Then compare the two rows. Ask which row looks like a message.
flow.say: Now a second set. Draw the dots again. Which set looks like a message? Which looks like random noise? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Listen again. Draw the dots. Which row looks like a message? Why?
flow.context: In this step, you listen to even taps and compare them with the uneven taps.

ask.q: Which set looks like a message, and why?
good: The even one, because it keeps a steady beat.
The second one. The gaps are all the same.

flow.parent: Say 'steady beat' rather than 'message'. We do not know what it means yet. We only know it is not random.

check.q: A row of dots has gaps that are all the same size. What is the best thing to say?
options: It looks like a signal, because a steady beat is unlikely to happen by chance
It is noise, because it is boring
It must be from a star
check.why: A steady beat is a pattern, and random noise rarely makes one. Jocelyn Bell noticed such a regular beat on her chart. A pattern does not tell us where it came from. We still need to check, for example, whether it comes back at the same time.

flow.do: Switch on a fan or a radio next to the helper. Ask them to tap the steady beat again. Ask your child to listen for it through the noise and draw the dots. Then ask how they could be sure the beat was there.
flow.parent: Measure how well it works. Before you start, ask your child to predict whether they will still hear the beat. Switch the fan or radio on low, then medium, then high, and ask the child to count the taps they heard out of 12 each time. Write the three counts. The count usually drops as the noise rises, and that gap shows how noise hides a signal. Keep the radio at a sensible volume to protect ears.
flow.say: Now there is background noise. Can you still hear the beat? How could you be sure, if you could not see the helper?
flow.kid: Noise is on. Can you still find the beat? How could you be sure?
flow.context: In this step, you add noise and try to find the signal in it. This is what scientists do with weak signals.

ask.q: How could you be sure the beat was there?
good: Listen again at another time.
Ask the helper to tap it again and see if it comes back.
Record it on a phone and listen again.

flow.think: A signal that comes back every time is much more believable than a one-off. How many times would you want it to come back?

activities.title: Can We Find Out? Sorting twelve questions

materials.item: 12 paper strips and a pencil
a big sheet of paper divided into three columns

schedule.what: Write the questions on strips. Sort them. Pick one and make an if-then prediction.

activities.record: A page with three columns and the questions sorted into them. Under it, one if-then sentence.
activities.context: In this activity, you sort twelve questions by the best way to answer them. Some can be tested, some can be looked up, and some need people to talk.

setup.art: Twelve paper strips with a question on each, lying in a pile beside a sheet of paper with three columns.
setup.caption: 1. Write the twelve questions on strips of paper.

setup.art: A child placing strips in three columns on a big sheet of paper headed test it, look it up, and talk about it.
setup.caption: 2. Sort the strips into three columns.

setup.art: A child writing an if-then sentence under a chosen question.
setup.caption: 3. Pick one question to test. Write an if-then sentence for it.

flow.do: Write these twelve questions on twelve strips. Which tumbler keeps ice longest, steel or plastic? How far away is the Moon? Is mango tastier than papaya? Do taller people have longer feet? Does the streetlight come on earlier on cloudy days? Is it fair that some schools have more books than others? How many drops fall from the tap in a minute? Which colour is the best colour? Does tulsi grow faster in the sun or in the shade? What did people eat 1000 years ago? Does a heavier ball always roll further? Is it kind to keep a bird in a cage?
flow.say: I have twelve questions. Some we can test at home. Some we can look up. Some are about taste or fairness, and people have to talk about them. Let's write them down.
flow.kid: Write twelve questions on strips. Some we can test. Some we can look up. Some need a talk.
flow.context: This is the first step of Can We Find Out. You write the twelve questions on strips of paper.
flow.parent: You can add your own questions. Children love to add silly ones. A good silly one is useful for the 'talk about it' column.

flow.do: Put three headings on the big sheet: 'Test it at home', 'Look it up or ask', and 'Talk about it'. Let your child place each strip in a column and say why. Some strips may fit in two columns.
flow.say: Which column does this question go in? Why? Is there another way to find out? If a question fits two columns, we can argue about it.
flow.kid: Put each strip in a column. Say why. Some fit two columns.
flow.context: In this step, you sort the questions into three columns.
flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, each child sorts a set of strips alone first, then compare and argue. With one child, you sort too and say why. Expect arguments, and enjoy them. The fairness and the cage questions are about what people value. A test cannot decide them alone, although evidence can help the talk.

check.q: 'Do taller people have longer feet?' Which column fits best?
options: Test it at home, by measuring many people
Talk about it
Look it up only
check.why: You can measure feet and heights of many people at home and look for a pattern. You could also look it up. It is not about taste or fairness, so it does not need a talk.

flow.do: Ask your child to pick one strip from the first column. Ask them to write two possible answers. Ask them to write an if-then sentence for each answer.
flow.say: Choose one question you can test. Write two possible answers. For each answer, write an if-then sentence about what you would see.
flow.kid: Pick one question. Write two answers. Write an if-then sentence for each.
flow.context: In this step, you turn one question into two rival ideas with predictions.
flow.think: Which question in the 'Talk about it' column would you most like to talk about with someone who disagrees?

activities.title: Draw the Invisible Water

materials.item: two sheets of plain paper
coloured pencils
a cold tumbler with drops on it (refill one with ice water if the Weeping Tumbler one has warmed up), or a picture of it

schedule.what: Draw what you think is happening. Read the explanation. Draw it again.

activities.record: Two drawings of the cold tumbler, one before and one after reading the explanation, with the differences circled.
activities.context: In this activity, you draw a model of what is happening in the air and on the tumbler wall. A model is a drawing that explains, including parts you cannot see.

setup.art: A child drawing a cold tumbler with the air around it and arrows showing where she thinks the water comes from.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the tumbler and the air around it. Show where you think the drops come from.

setup.art: A child reading a page with a picture of water vapour dots in the air landing on a cold tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Read the explanation about water vapour.

setup.art: A second drawing next to the first, with the differences circled in red.
setup.caption: 3. Draw it again and circle what changed.

flow.do: Give your child a sheet of paper. Ask them to draw the cold tumbler, the air around it and the drops. Ask them to draw arrows to show where they think the water comes from. Include the parts you cannot see.
flow.say: Draw the cold tumbler, the air around it and the drops. Draw arrows to show where the water comes from. Draw the parts we cannot see too.
flow.kid: Draw the tumbler, the air and the drops. Draw arrows for the water.
flow.context: This is the first step of Draw the Invisible Water. You draw what you think is happening.
flow.parent: Do not correct the drawing. Any drawing is a good start. Ask about the arrows.

flow.do: Read the card 'Why drops form on the outside of a cold tumbler' aloud. Then give your child a second sheet to draw it again with new ideas.
flow.say: Here is what scientists say. Let's read it. Now draw it again. What would you add or change?
flow.kid: Read the card. Draw it again. What do you change?
flow.context: In this step, you read the explanation and draw a better model.

ask.q: What did you add the second time?
good: Water vapour in the air.
Arrows from the air to the steel.
Cold air near the wall.

check.q: In a model of a cold tumbler, what is missing if you only draw the tumbler and the drops?
options: The air with water vapour in it
A bigger tumbler
The colour of the drops
check.why: The drops come from invisible water vapour in the air. A model that leaves out the air leaves out the main actor.

flow.do: Put the two drawings side by side. Ask your child to circle what is different. Ask which parts they could not see, but they now know are there.
flow.say: Put your two drawings side by side. Circle what is different. Which parts can you not see, but you now know are there?
flow.kid: Put your two drawings side by side. Circle what changed.
flow.context: In this step, you compare your first and second model.
flow.think: A model is not a photograph. It shows what we think is going on, including the parts we cannot see. Use your second drawing to predict: would a cold tumbler sweat as much in a dry room? Write your prediction in an if-then sentence, then test it if you can: compare a cold tumbler in the kitchen with one in a room with an air conditioner. Each child can draw their own model, then compare them.

activities.title: Two Ideas for Something at Home

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
something at home that puzzles you, such as a wobbling fan, a humming lift, a dripping tap or a noisy pipe

schedule.what: Pick a puzzle. Write what you saw. Write two rival ideas. Find a deciding question.

activities.record: A page with the puzzle, what you saw, two rival ideas with if-then sentences, and one deciding question.
activities.context: In this activity, you pick a real puzzle from home and plan how to tell two ideas apart.

setup.art: A child standing in front of a wobbling ceiling fan with a notebook, writing what she sees.
setup.caption: 1. Pick something at home that puzzles you. Write what you saw.

setup.art: A notebook page with two boxes headed Idea A and Idea B and an if-then sentence in each box.
setup.caption: 2. Write two rival ideas. Write an if-then sentence for each.

setup.art: A child holding a finger up at a fork in a path with a question mark above it.
setup.caption: 3. Find a question the two ideas answer differently.

flow.do: Walk around your home with your child for two minutes. Ask them to pick something that puzzles them. Ask them to write three observations about it, with no 'because'.
flow.say: Let's find something that puzzles you. A fan, a tap, a sound, a smell. Write three things you can see or hear about it. Do not use the word because.
flow.kid: Find something that puzzles you. Write three things you notice. No 'because'.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Ideas for Something at Home. You pick a puzzle and write what you saw.
flow.parent: Good puzzles include a noisy fan, a dripping tap, a door that sticks, damp on a wall, or a humming fridge. With 2 to 4 children, each can pick a puzzle, or the group can choose one and write ideas separately. Then compare whose ideas differ.

check.q: Which of these is an observation about a dripping tap?
options: It drips about twice every five seconds
The washer is worn
It is trying to annoy us
check.why: Counting drips is something you saw. A worn washer and an annoyed tap are stories about why.

flow.do: Ask your child to write two rival ideas for the puzzle. Under each idea, write an if-then sentence about something else they would see.
flow.say: What is one idea about why it happens? Is there a different idea? If your first idea is true, what else would you see? And if the second is true?
flow.kid: Write two ideas. For each, write an if-then sentence.
flow.context: In this step, you write two rival ideas and what each one predicts.

ask.q: What would you see if idea A is true that you would not see for idea B?
good: Something that only happens with A.
A different sound or a different time.

flow.do: Ask your child to choose the question that the two ideas answer differently. Ask whether they can check it safely at home, with a grown-up. If they can, do it now or tomorrow.
flow.say: Which of your if-then sentences gives a different result for the two ideas? That is your deciding question. Can we check it safely?
flow.kid: Find the question the two ideas answer differently. Can you check it safely?
flow.context: In this step, you find the deciding question for your own puzzle.
flow.parent: Only check things that are safe. Do not touch electricity, hot things or anything at height. A grown-up can switch things off. If it cannot be checked at home, ask or look it up.

projects.title: Streetlight Detective: timer or light sensor?

materials.item: a window or balcony that looks at a streetlight, a security light or a lamp that comes on by itself in the evening
a phone or watch to read the time
a notebook and a pencil
a phone weather app or a newspaper that shows sunset time

projects.safety: Watch from inside a window or behind the balcony railing. Do not lean out. A grown-up should be home in the evening. Do not go onto the road or touch any light, pole or wire.

schedule.what: Choose the light. Write the rival ideas and your if-then predictions. Draw the table.
Write the time the light comes on, the sky and the sunset time.
Write the time the light comes on, the sky and the sunset time.
Write the time the light comes on, the sky and the sunset time.
Write the time the light comes on, the sky and the sunset time.
Write the time the light comes on, the sky and the sunset time. Look out for a cloudy evening.
Look at the whole table. Decide which idea fits and what you cannot say.

projects.record: A table with the date, the weather, the sunset time, the time the light came on and the difference. At the end, one sentence about what you found and one about what you cannot say.
projects.context: In this project, you watch a light that comes on by itself at dusk, for a week, and use a deciding day to tell two ideas apart.

setup.art: A child at a window with a notebook looking at a streetlight in the distance at dusk.
setup.caption: 1. Choose a light you can see from inside. Write the rival ideas.

setup.art: A notebook table with columns for date, weather, sunset time, time the light came on, and difference.
setup.caption: 2. Each evening, write the time the light comes on.

setup.art: A cloudy dark evening with the streetlight already glowing and a phone showing 5:40 pm.
setup.caption: 3. Look out for a dark, cloudy evening. This is your deciding day.

flow.do: 1. Choose a light that comes on by itself, such as a streetlight or a security light. 2. Write two ideas. Idea A: a timer switches it on at the same clock time every day. Idea B: a light sensor switches it on when it gets dark. 3. Write an if-then sentence for each, for a very cloudy evening. 4. Draw the table.
flow.say: Some lights come on by themselves. Maybe a timer switches them on at the same time every day. Maybe a sensor switches them on when it is dark. What would you see on a dark, cloudy evening for each idea?
flow.kid: Choose a light. Write two ideas. Timer or sensor? What happens on a cloudy day?
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Streetlight Detective. You choose the light and plan.

ask.q: What would each idea show on a dark, cloudy evening?
good: A timer would switch the light on at the usual time.
A sensor would switch the light on earlier, because it is dark sooner.

flow.parent: Some lights are switched by a person, or by a timer that moves with the seasons. Whatever you find is a real result. Write 'could not see' on any evening you miss.

check.q: Sunset is at 6:00 pm. On a clear evening the light comes on at 6:10 pm. On a very cloudy evening it comes on at 5:35 pm. Which idea fits?
options: Light sensor, because the time changed with the darkness
Timer, because the light came on
Neither
check.why: A timer would switch it on at the same clock time on both evenings. The light came on earlier when the sky was darker, which fits a sensor better. One cloudy day is a good clue. More days make it stronger.

flow.do: Each evening for the next five days, write the date, the sky, the sunset time and the time the light came on. Work out the difference between the sunset time and the time the light came on.
flow.say: Watch the light from about twenty minutes before sunset. Write what time it comes on. Look at the sky. Was it clear or cloudy?
flow.kid: Each evening, write the time the light comes on. Is the sky clear or cloudy?
flow.context: In these days, you collect a week of evidence about when the light comes on.
flow.parent: Look at the light for ten minutes around the usual time. If you miss an evening, write 'missed'. Do not guess. A phone weather app often shows the sunset time. With 2 to 4 children, share jobs each evening: one reads the sunset time, one watches the light, one judges the sky, one writes. Swap daily. Many city lights come on a little after sunset, and some are switched by hand or by a central timer, so whatever you see is a real result. Sunset moves by only a minute or less a day, so a week of the same clock time may still fit a timer. In dry months you may not get a cloudy evening. Then look at how the gap between sunset and light-on changes, and say honestly that you could not tell the ideas apart.
flow.wait: Do this each evening for the next five days.

flow.do: On day 7, look at the whole table. Mark the cloudiest evening. Ask which idea fits the evidence. Ask what cannot be said from only one week.
flow.say: Look at the cloudiest evening. When did the light come on that day? What does that say about the two ideas? What can you not say from one week?
flow.kid: Look at your week. Which idea fits? What can't you say?
flow.context: In this step, you decide which idea the evidence supports and what it cannot tell you.

ask.q: Which idea does your evidence support, and what can't you say?
good: The light follows the dark, so it is a sensor. I only watched one light.
It came on at the same time every day, so it is a timer. But I did not have a really dark day.

flow.think: If you had no cloudy evenings, could you still tell the ideas apart? What else could you look at?

challenges.title: Does the Fridge Light Stay On? A puzzle you cannot look at
challenges.problem: When you close the fridge door, does the light inside go off or stay on? You cannot look, because opening the door lets in the room light. Design a test that can tell the two ideas apart.
constraints: Do not leave the fridge door open for more than a few seconds.
Do not take the fridge apart or touch anything electrical.
A grown-up must help with the phone and the fridge door.
Your test must give a different result if the light is on and if it is off.
materials: a phone that can record video
a dark cupboard or a drawer that closes
general: Record a video of the inside of the fridge with a phone, close the door for 30 seconds and open it again. Check whether the video shows light.
Do the same in a dark cupboard, as a control. Compare how bright the two videos are.
creative: Turn the phone screen to its lowest brightness and face the screen away from the camera's view, so the screen does not light the picture.
Compare the brightness of three videos: the fridge, the dark cupboard and the open room, so you can see what 'dark' and 'light' look like.
Repeat the whole test with the phone in a different place on the shelf. A result that comes back the same way is stronger than a result you saw once.
challenges.safety: A grown-up opens and closes the fridge door and handles the phone. Keep the door shut for only about 30 seconds so the food stays cool. Take the phone out straight away, because it should not get very cold. Make sure the phone and any wire are not caught in the door seal, and do not use a phone that is plugged in.
challenges.your_turn: Now think of another thing you cannot look at without changing it, such as a closed room, a sleeping baby or a sealed box. Design a test to tell two ideas apart.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a test for a puzzle where looking changes the answer.

setup.art: A child holding a phone next to the open fridge while a grown-up holds the door.
setup.caption: 1. Write the two ideas and what each predicts.

setup.art: A phone set on a fridge shelf facing the door, with its screen turned down.
setup.caption: 2. Place the phone inside the fridge and start a video.

setup.art: A phone recording in a dark cupboard, next to the notebook with two results compared.
setup.caption: 3. Do the same in a dark cupboard and compare the two videos.

flow.do: Write the two ideas. Idea A: the light goes off when the door closes. Idea B: the light stays on when the door closes. Ask your child what is hard about checking. Ask for their design.
flow.say: Two ideas. The light goes off when the door shuts. Or the light stays on. Why can't we just look? How could we find out without opening the door?
flow.kid: Two ideas about the fridge light. Why can't you just look? How could you find out?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fridge Light challenge. You plan your design.

ask.q: Why can't we just open the door and look?
good: Opening the door might switch the light on.
The room light gets in.
We would change the thing we want to look at.

flow.do: 1. Switch the phone to video. 2. Turn the screen brightness to the lowest. 3. Place the phone on a fridge shelf with the camera facing the door. 4. Start the video, close the door and wait 30 seconds. 5. Open the door, stop the video and take the phone out. 6. Do the same in the dark cupboard.
flow.say: Phone on the shelf, camera facing the door. Start the video. Close the door. Count to thirty. Open the door. Now do the same in the dark cupboard.
flow.kid: Put the phone in the fridge. Record. Close the door. Wait 30 seconds. Do it in the cupboard too.
flow.context: In this step, you record the inside of the fridge and the inside of a dark cupboard.
flow.parent: The phone screen glows, so the control matters. The cupboard video shows what the phone's own glow looks like. If the fridge video is brighter than the cupboard video, the light stayed on. Keep the door shut only for 30 seconds so the food stays cool. Take the phone out straight away, because it should not get very cold.

flow.do: Watch both videos. Ask which one is brighter. Ask what that shows. Ask what else they could try.
flow.say: Watch the two videos. Which is brighter? What does that tell us about the fridge light?
flow.kid: Watch the two videos. Which is brighter? What does that show?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the two videos and say what they show.
flow.parent: For most fridges, the video from inside the closed fridge is as dark as the cupboard video, because a small switch in the door puts the light out when the door is shut. A phone camera brightens dark pictures by itself, so both videos may look grainy grey. Compare them with the first seconds of the fridge video, taken with the door still open, which should look clearly brighter. If your result differs, repeat it, and note it down. With 2 to 4 children, one holds the timer, one watches the video, and one writes, and everyone predicts before watching.

check.q: The fridge video is as dark as the cupboard video. What does this suggest?
options: The fridge light goes off when the door is closed
The fridge light stays on
The phone broke
check.why: The cupboard video shows how dark it looks when there is only the phone's own glow. If the fridge looked the same, there was no extra light, so the fridge light was off. The cupboard video was the control.

items.p: Which sentence is an observation about a steel tumbler of ice water?
opts: The tumbler leaked
There are small clear drops on the outside of the tumbler
The ice made the steel sweat
items.why: An observation is what you can see, and anyone can check it. 'Leaked' and 'made the steel sweat' are stories about why the drops are there. They are inferences.

items.p: Sort each sentence about a bowl of curd on the shelf. Is it something you saw, or something you think?
items.why: Sentences that report what you see, feel or count belong in 'I saw'. Sentences about why something happened, or what someone did, are stories. They belong in 'I think', until a test checks them.
items: There is a thin watery layer on top of the curd
The bowl is cold to touch
Someone left the fridge door open
A few small bubbles are in the curd
The curd was made with too much starter

items.p: Mira says, 'Every inference is wrong, so scientists should never make one.' Is she right?
items.why: False. Inferences are guesses made from what we saw, and science is full of them. The point is to know which sentences are inferences, so we can test them.

items.p: Kavya sees her money plant leaning towards the window. Which sentence is an inference?
opts: The leaves are pointing to the window
The plant wants the sunlight
The pot is on the sill
items.why: 'Wants the sunlight' is a guess about why the plant leans. The leaves pointing and the pot on the sill can both be seen. Plants do bend towards light, and a lamp test could check this.

items.p: Two different explanations for the same thing you saw are called ____ explanations.
items.why: Rival explanations compete. Usually at most one of them is right, so we look for a way to choose between them.

items.p: Meenakshi's dosa batter did not rise overnight. Write two different explanations that could both fit.
items.a: For example: the kitchen was too cold. Or: there was not enough time. Or: the batter was too thick. Any two sensible, different explanations score.
items.why: A good answer gives two ideas that are different from each other and that could each be checked, for example by keeping batter in a warm place and in a cold place.

items.p: Farhan says ants find the sugar by smell. Arjun says they follow a trail left by other ants. Which check can tell the ideas apart?
opts: Count how many ants arrive
Wipe a short piece of the ants' path and watch what they do
Give the ants a bigger piece of sugar
items.why: If the ants follow a trail, wiping a piece of it will confuse them. If they find the sugar alone by smell, they will carry on. Counting or giving more sugar gives the same result under both ideas.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These words come up in every investigation. A strong answer could give an example for each one.
pairs: what you notice, without adding why
a guess you work out from what you noticed
what you expect to see if an idea is true
what you saw that counts for or against an idea

items.p: Put the steps of telling two ideas apart in the best order.
a: Notice something odd and write what you saw
Write an if-then sentence for each idea
Find a question the ideas answer differently
Do the check and write what you saw
items.why: You need something to explain first. Then you need ideas, then what each one predicts. Only then can you find the question where they differ and do the check.
items: Find a question the ideas answer differently
Do the check and write what you saw
Notice something odd and write what you saw
Write an if-then sentence for each idea

items.p: If both ideas predict exactly the same result, a test cannot choose between them.
items.why: True. If both ideas give the same result, any result fits both. You need a check where the two ideas give different results.

items.p: Which is the best if-then prediction for the idea 'The pigeons leave because of the bell'?
opts: If the bell scares the pigeons, they will leave later
If the bell scares the pigeons, they will stay on an evening when the bell does not ring
If the bell scares the pigeons, they will fly high
items.why: A good prediction says what you will see if the idea is true, and could be shown wrong. If the pigeons leave without the bell, the idea is in trouble.

items.p: Three of these ideas can be tested. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: The drops on the tumbler come from the air
The pigeons leave because of the dusk
The tumbler is wet because an invisible helper makes it wet, and hides when we look
The curd sets faster in a warm place
items.why: The invisible helper fits every possible result, so no test could show it wrong. The other three say something that a check could contradict.

items.p: Draw two columns headed 'I saw' and 'I think'. Write three sentences about a crow on your railing in the correct columns.
items.a: A page with two columns. Under 'I saw': for example, 'A crow sits on the railing' and 'The crow turns their head'. Under 'I think': for example, 'The crow is hungry'.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps what can be seen apart from the reasons we add. 'The crow is waiting for food' belongs in the second column.
items.art: A notebook page with two columns, one headed I saw and one headed I think, and a crow drawn on a railing.

items.p: In a tumbler test, a girl colours the water inside red. The drops on the outside are clear. What is the best conclusion?
opts: The drops did not come from the water inside
Colour cannot go through steel
The red colour was too weak
items.why: If the water inside had crossed the steel, the drops would carry the colour. They are clear, so the water came from somewhere else. The air is the likely source.

items.p: A girl's test gives a result she did not expect. She wants to rub it out and write what she thought would happen. Her brother wants to keep it and repeat the test. Who do you agree with?
items.a: A strong answer keeps the odd result, writes it down as it is and repeats the test, and also gives the girl's worry a fair hearing.
items.why: Pick-a-side questions have no single right side. Marks go for using the idea of evidence and for stating the other view fairly.

views.says: An odd number will make my page look wrong. Maybe I made a slip. Let me write what I expected.
Keep it exactly as it is, and test again. If it happens again, it is real. If not, we can say it was probably a slip.

items.ask: Do you rub it out or keep it, and what would you do next?

items.p: Why is it better to write a prediction before the test than after it?
items.a: Once you have seen the result, it is easy to believe you expected it all along. A written prediction is fixed, so the test can really show you wrong.
items.why: A strong answer says that the written prediction cannot change after the result, so we can trust it as a test of the idea.

items.p: On a normal day, why does a tumbler of warm water stay dry on the outside?
opts: The air next to a warm tumbler stays warm, so its water vapour does not turn into drops
Warm water has no vapour
Warm water is too heavy to leak
items.why: Drops form when air touches something cold enough to turn some of its vapour into liquid. A warm tumbler does not cool the air next to it.

items.p: A cold bottle from the fridge gets wet outside in a damp kitchen but stays almost dry in a very dry winter room. What is the best reason?
opts: Dry air has less water vapour to collect
The bottle leaks more in summer
The fridge is cold only in summer
items.why: Condensation needs vapour in the air. When the air is dry, there is less vapour, so fewer drops form and they come more slowly.

items.p: Choose the best way of finding out for each question.
items.why: A fair test changes one thing. A pattern search measures many cases. A long watch looks again and again over time. Looking it up suits questions we cannot check at home.
items: Does more salt in water help a potato float?
Do taller children have longer feet?
When does the school bus come each morning?
How far away is the Sun?
Does a bigger paper helicopter fall slower?
How many petals do hibiscus flowers have?

items.p: If two things go together, one must cause the other.
items.why: False. A third thing can cause both, or it can be chance. Shoe size and reading skill go together in primary school because both grow with age.

items.p: Priya measured 8 people. Seven had an arm span within 4 centimetres of their height. One had a span 12 centimetres more than the height. What should Priya do about the odd one, and why?
items.a: Measure that person again, check the tape was straight, and write down both results. If it is the same again, keep it. Do not rub it out.
items.why: A good answer says to check and repeat before deciding, and to keep the record honest whatever the second measurement shows.

items.p: Which gives a steadier pattern about arm span and height?
opts: Measuring 3 people
Measuring 12 people
Measuring only the tallest person
items.why: More cases give a steadier pattern, because any one person may be a little odd. Measuring only one kind of person is also unfair.

items.p: The small wobble in any measurement, from where you hold the tape or how you read it, is called measurement ____.
items.why: Measurement error is not a mistake. It is the small difference you get when you measure the same thing twice. Every measurement has some.

items.p: Ice cream sales and sunburn cases both go up in summer. What is the best explanation?
opts: Ice cream causes sunburn
Hot sunny weather causes both
Sunburn makes people buy ice cream
items.why: A third thing, the hot sunny weather, can explain both. Two things that go up together do not have to cause each other.

items.p: Put the steps of a long watch in order.
a: Choose what to watch and why
Choose when and how often to look
Look and write each result with the time
Lay the results side by side
Say what the pattern shows and what it cannot show
items.why: A long watch needs a plan first, then regular looks recorded with the time, and only at the end the pattern and what it can and cannot say.
items: Lay the results side by side
Choose what to watch and why
Say what the pattern shows and what it cannot show
Look and write each result with the time
Choose when and how often to look

items.p: Eight people had these differences between arm span and height, in centimetres: 0, +2, −1, +3, −4, +1, 0, +12. Draw a number line from −5 to +15 and put a dot for each person. Circle the one that does not fit.
items.a: A number line from −5 to +15 with seven dots near zero and one dot at +12, circled.
items.why: A dot graph shows that most people are close to zero and one is far away. The far dot should be checked and repeated, not hidden.
items.art: A number line from minus five to plus fifteen with eight dots, seven close to zero and one far to the right.

items.p: Match each question to the best way of finding out.
items.why: Questions about change over time need regular looks. Questions about what goes with what need many cases. Questions about what one thing does need a fair test. Questions we cannot test at home can be looked up.
pairs: Does the streetlight come on earlier on cloudy days?
Do taller people have longer arms?
Does lemon juice slow browning of cut fruit?

items.p: Three of these are good ways to handle a surprising result. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Check how the test was done
Repeat the test
Rub it out because it does not fit
Write it down exactly as it was
items.why: Rubbing out an odd result hides the very thing that may teach us something. The other three are what careful scientists do.

items.p: The warm tumbler also gets a few drops after 15 minutes. What should you do first?
opts: Check whether the room is very humid and whether the water has cooled
Rub out the observation
Say the idea about air is wrong
items.why: A surprising result needs checking. A humid room or water that has cooled can make a few drops on a warm tumbler. You write it down and compare with the cold tumbler.

items.p: Two friends measure many people and find that arm span and height are close, but never exactly equal. One says the old drawing by Leonardo, which showed them equal, was wrong. The other says it was a good rule of thumb. Who do you agree with?
items.a: A strong answer says that 'close' and 'exactly' are different claims, and that a good claim says which one it makes. Both friends have a point.
items.why: Pick-a-side questions have no single right side. Marks go for using evidence from the measuring and for stating the other view fairly.

views.says: Leonardo drew them exactly equal. Real people are not exactly equal, so the drawing was wrong.
A rule that is close for most people is still useful. It is a good guide, as long as we say close, not exactly.

items.ask: Is a rule that is almost always close 'right' or 'wrong'?

items.p: Two ideas both fit everything you saw so far. Explain in your own words why watching more of the same cannot choose between them.
items.a: Both ideas expect the same results, so every new result fits both. You need a situation where the ideas expect different results.
items.why: A good answer says that the ideas have to disagree about something for a test to separate them.

items.p: A surprising result should be rubbed out so the page looks tidy.
items.why: False. The surprising result may be the discovery. Check it, repeat it and keep the record.

items.p: A strange mark on a chart comes back about four minutes earlier each day by the clock. What does that suggest?
opts: It follows star time, so it may come from the sky
It follows the clock on the wall, so it is a machine on Earth
It was drawn by someone
items.why: Things in the sky return about four minutes earlier each day. Machines on Earth follow the clock on the wall. This is the test Jocelyn Bell's team used.

items.p: A crackle on a radio comes at exactly 7 pm every day by the clock. What does that suggest?
opts: It probably comes from something that works on the clock, such as a neighbour's machine
It comes from a distant star
It is a message from space
items.why: Anything that returns at the same clock time each day follows human routines. A star would drift earlier each day.

items.p: A damp patch grows on the wall under the terrace. Idea A: rain is seeping in. Idea B: a pipe is leaking. Write a deciding question and say what each idea predicts.
items.a: Does the patch grow on a long dry spell? If rain, it will stop growing on dry days. If a pipe, it will keep growing on dry days too.
items.why: A strong answer chooses something about which the ideas disagree and says what each would show.

items.p: Which of these ideas could a test show wrong?
items.why: An idea that fits every possible result cannot be tested. A testable idea says what you will see, so a different result can show it wrong.
items: The drops come from the air
The light is switched on by a timer
Something invisible makes everything happen, whatever we see
The pigeons leave because of the bell
It happens because it was always going to happen

items.p: A research student sees a strange mark on a chart and her supervisor receives the biggest prize for the discovery. Should the person who first noticed the mark have her name on the prize?
items.a: A strong answer weighs both views and says what counts as discovering something. Real prizes have often gone to supervisors, and many scientists now say students deserved more credit.
items.why: Pick-a-side questions have no single right side. Marks go for fairly stating both views and giving a reason.

views.says: The one who noticed and followed the mark is the discoverer. Her name belongs on the prize.
A prize goes to the person who led the work and took responsibility. The student helped, but the leader's plan made the discovery possible.

items.ask: Whose name should be on a discovery, and why?

items.p: Which sentence is a good if-then prediction?
opts: If the light is a timer, it will come on at the same clock time on a very cloudy evening
If the light is a timer, it will come on
If it is cloudy, I will be sad
items.why: A good prediction names the idea, the situation and the result you expect. It could turn out wrong.

items.p: An idea that fits every possible result is the strongest kind of idea.
items.why: False. An idea that fits every result tells you nothing about this case and cannot be tested. A strong idea says what you will see, so it can be wrong.

items.p: A question that two explanations answer differently is called a ____ question.
items.why: A deciding question is the heart of telling ideas apart. If both ideas give the same answer, the question cannot decide.

items.p: Three of these questions could tell the tumbler ideas apart. Which one cannot?
opts: What colour are the drops if the water inside is coloured?
Do the drops appear on a warm tumbler?
Do the drops come back when you wipe a patch dry?
How many ice cubes did we use?
items.why: The number of ice cubes does not separate leaking from water in the air. The other three give different results under the two ideas.

items.p: Put these in a good order for handling a surprising result.
a: Check how the test was done
Write down exactly what you saw
Ask what the surprise could mean
items.why: Write it down first so it cannot disappear. Then look for a slip, then repeat, and only then think about what it could mean.

items.p: Match each word about measurements to what it means.
items.why: These words help us talk about measurements that are hard to read. A strong answer could give an example for each.

items.p: A scientist wants to know how old the Moon is. Which way of finding out is best?
opts: A fair test at home
Looking it up in the work of other scientists
Asking five friends to vote
items.why: We cannot change the Moon or watch its whole history at home. Other scientists have measured the age with rock samples and careful reasoning, and we can read what they found.

items.p: Describe a pattern you could look for with a measuring tape and ten people. Say what you would measure, and what you could not say from the result.
items.a: For example: foot length and height. We could say whether taller people tend to have longer feet. We could not say whether height causes long feet, or whether this is true for everyone in the world.
items.why: A strong answer names two things to measure and says what the result would show and what it could not show.

items.p: Draw a model of the mist that appears on a bathroom mirror after a hot shower. Show the air, the water vapour, the mirror and where the drops come from.
items.a: A mirror with warm moist air near it, dots of vapour, and tiny drops forming on the cooler glass.
items.why: A good model shows invisible vapour in the air and the cooler glass turning some of it into drops. It is the same idea as the cold tumbler.
items.art: A bathroom mirror with dots of water vapour in the air arrowing to tiny drops forming on its surface.

items.p: A girl says, 'I have watched the same thing for a year and it always fits both my ideas, so I know both are true.' What is wrong with this?
opts: Fitting both ideas does not show either is true, because the watching cannot separate them
A year is too short
She should have watched less
items.why: When every result fits both ideas, the results cannot tell the ideas apart. She needs a day when the ideas disagree.

items.p: A friend says a rain dance brings rain because it rained twice after a dance. Write two rival explanations and one deciding question.
items.a: Explanation A: the dance brought the rain. Explanation B: it was going to rain anyway. Deciding question: does it also rain on days when nobody dances, and how often?
items.why: A good answer compares days with and without the dance. Two cases cannot decide, because rain is common.

quiz.p: Which of these is an inference about a wet tumbler?
opts: The outside is covered in small drops
The steel is sweating because it is hot inside
The tumbler is on a plate
quiz.why: 'Sweating because it is hot inside' is a story about why. Even the idea of the tumbler 'sweating' is a story. The drops and the plate can be seen.

quiz.p: Two ideas both fit everything you have seen. What will help you choose between them?
opts: Watching the same thing for longer
Finding a situation where the ideas predict different things
Voting on which idea is nicer
quiz.why: More of the same watching gives results that fit both ideas. A situation where they disagree can separate them.

quiz.p: A girl colours the water inside a cold tumbler. What would show that the drops on the outside came from the air?
opts: The drops are coloured
The drops are clear
There are no drops
quiz.why: If the water had leaked through, the drops would carry the colour. Clear drops fit the air idea.

quiz.p: Which is the best if-then prediction for 'the streetlight is switched by a timer'?
opts: If it is a timer, the light will come on at the same clock time on a dark cloudy evening
If it is a timer, the light will glow
If it is a timer, the sky will be dark
quiz.why: A good prediction names the idea, the situation and what you will see, and it could be wrong.

quiz.p: Which idea is the hardest to test?
opts: The drops come from the air
Something invisible makes it happen, whatever we see
The light is switched by a sensor
quiz.why: An idea that fits every possible result cannot be shown wrong, so no test can use it.

quiz.p: A mark on a chart comes back at the same time by the clock every day. What does this suggest?
opts: It follows human routines, such as a machine
It comes from a star
It was made by the Moon
quiz.why: Things that follow the clock on the wall are usually made by people. A signal from the stars comes back about four minutes earlier each day.

quiz.p: Arman measured the arm span and height of 8 people. The two numbers were close for almost everyone. What can he say?
opts: In the people he measured, arm span was close to height
Everyone in the world has an arm span equal to their height
A long arm span makes you taller
quiz.why: A small sample can show what is true for those people, and hint at a pattern. It cannot speak for everyone, and it cannot show which thing causes which.

quiz.p: Which question is best answered by a long watch?
opts: Does lemon juice slow browning of cut fruit?
Do the pigeons leave earlier each week as the days shorten?
How far is the Sun?
quiz.why: A long watch looks at the same thing again and again over time. Browning needs a fair test, and the Sun's distance can be looked up.

quiz.p: A test gives a result nobody expected. What is the best first step?
opts: Rub it out
Check how the test was done and repeat it
Change the idea to match
quiz.why: A surprise might be a slip, or it might be a discovery. Checking and repeating shows which.

quiz.p: Two things go up together in summer: ice cream sales and sunburn. Which statement is best?
opts: Ice cream causes sunburn
Hot sunny weather may cause both
Sunburn causes ice cream
quiz.why: A third thing can cause both. Going up together is a pattern, not proof of a cause.

quiz.p: Why do we write predictions before a test?
opts: So we cannot change our minds about what we expected after seeing the result
So the test runs faster
So the answer is always right
quiz.why: A written prediction cannot be changed by the result. That keeps the test honest.

quiz.p: A warm tumbler of water stays dry outside while a cold one gets wet. What does this show about the drops?
opts: The cold steel matters, because the same air made no drops on the warm one
Warm water cannot leak
The tumblers were different sizes
quiz.why: Same air and same room, but different temperatures, so the cold made the difference.

open_questions.q: How exactly do birds judge that evening is coming, and how do they add up light, their body clock and the street lights?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that light matters and that birds have light-sensitive cells in the eye and deep in the brain. How the pieces combine is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How do pulsars make their beams of radio waves?
open_questions.why_open: Astronomers know pulsars are spinning, tiny, dense stars. How the radio beam is made is still debated.

open_questions.q: Is there any question that no test could ever answer?
open_questions.why_open: Some thinkers say yes, for example questions about what happened before time began. Others say we have not yet found the right test.

open_questions.q: Do other animals ask questions and test their own ideas?
open_questions.why_open: Some animals, such as crows and apes, solve new puzzles in ways that look like trying out ideas. Whether this is asking a question as we do is still debated.

open_questions.q: Can a very good question be asked by someone who does not yet know any science?
open_questions.why_open: Children ask some of the deepest questions. Whether asking well can be taught, and how, is still being studied by people who research learning.

open_questions.q: Why do people stay with an idea after a test has shown it wrong?
open_questions.why_open: Psychologists have found many reasons, such as habit and pride. Nobody has a complete answer or a sure cure.

maths.problem: Aadhira is 132 centimetres tall and her arm span is 129 centimetres. What is her span minus her height?
maths.explain: 129 minus 132 is minus 3. The negative sign means her span is 3 centimetres shorter than her height.
maths.context: In the Arm Span test, you measure height and arm span and work out span minus height for each person.
maths.why_maths: A negative number tells you which one is longer as well as by how much, so you can compare people easily.

maths.problem: Eight people had these differences between arm span and height, in centimetres: 0, +2, −1, +3, −4, +1, 0, +12. How many were within 3 centimetres of zero? Which one is the odd one out, and by how much is it more than the next biggest?
maths.answer: Six were within 3 centimetres of zero. The odd one is +12, which is 9 more than +3.
maths.explain: The numbers 0, +2, −1, +3, +1 and 0 are within 3 of zero. That is six. The number −4 is 4 away from zero, so it is outside. The biggest is +12 and the next biggest is +3. 12 minus 3 is 9.
maths.context: After the Arm Span test, you look at the differences to see which numbers sit close together and which one is far away.
maths.why_maths: Counting how many numbers are close to zero shows whether a pattern is steady. A number far from the others tells you what to check and measure again.

maths.problem: A cold tumbler had 12 drops on its outside after 5 minutes, 30 after 10 minutes and 55 after 15 minutes. How many new drops formed between each look? What does this tell you about the speed?
maths.answer: 18 new drops in the second five minutes, and 25 new drops in the third. The drops are forming faster.
maths.explain: 30 minus 12 is 18. 55 minus 30 is 25. The first five minutes gave 12 drops, then 18, then 25. The number of new drops each five minutes is going up.
maths.context: In the Weeping Tumbler test, you look at the cold tumbler at 5, 10 and 15 minutes. Here are example counts of the drops in one small square, made up to practise subtraction.
maths.why_maths: Comparing how many new drops appear in each time gap shows whether the change is speeding up or slowing down.

maths.problem: A height of 125 centimetres has a measurement wobble of 2 centimetres. About how many in every 100 centimetres is that wobble?
maths.explain: 2 out of 125 is 1.6 out of 100, which is about 2 out of 100. It is a small wobble compared with the height.
maths.context: In the Arm Span test, each measurement may be a centimetre or two out, and you need to know if that matters.
maths.why_maths: Turning the wobble into a share of the whole shows whether it is big or small, so you know whether to trust the pattern.

maths.problem: A bright star crosses a window at 8:00 pm tonight. A star comes back about 4 minutes earlier each day. At about what time will it cross in 5 days?
maths.explain: 4 minutes earlier each day for 5 days is 4 times 5, which is 20 minutes. 20 minutes before 8:00 pm is 7:40 pm.
maths.context: Jocelyn Bell's team told a signal from the sky from a machine on Earth by seeing that the signal came back about four minutes earlier each day.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the daily shift by the number of days predicts when a star will return, so you can check if a signal follows star time.

maths.problem: A star crossed a window at 8:00 pm. After 14 days, about how much earlier will it cross, and about what time?
maths.answer: About 56 minutes earlier, so about 7:04 pm.
maths.explain: 4 times 14 is 56 minutes. 8:00 pm take away 56 minutes is 7:04 pm. After about two weeks the star comes back nearly an hour earlier.
maths.context: Things in the sky return about four minutes earlier each day, which is how a signal from the sky can be told from a machine.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a small daily change shows how it adds up over weeks, which is why a long watch can reveal a slow drift.

maths.problem: On a dark cloudy evening the streetlight came on at 5:35 pm. On a clear evening it came on at 6:10 pm. How many minutes earlier was it on the cloudy evening?
maths.explain: From 5:35 pm to 6:00 pm is 25 minutes. From 6:00 pm to 6:10 pm is 10 more minutes. 25 plus 10 is 35.
maths.context: In the Streetlight Detective project, you compare the time the light comes on during a clear evening and a very cloudy evening.
maths.why_maths: The size of the time gap tells you whether the light followed the darkness or the clock, which separates the two ideas.

maths.problem: In a sample of 6 people, 5 had an arm span within 3 centimetres of their height. If the same share held for 60 people, how many would that be?
maths.explain: 5 out of 6 is the same share as 50 out of 60, because 6 times 10 is 60 and 5 times 10 is 50.
maths.context: After measuring a small group, you may wonder what a larger group would look like.
maths.why_maths: Scaling a share up to a bigger group shows what the pattern would mean for more people, if it stayed the same. It also shows why we need to measure more to be sure.

maths.problem: In one class, 3 of 4 nine-year-olds wore big shoes, and 1 of 4 six-year-olds did. Older children also read better. Compare the two shares. Could age explain both big shoes and better reading?
maths.answer: Big shoes were three times as common among the nine-year-olds. Yes, age could explain both.
maths.explain: 3 out of 4 is 75 out of 100 and 1 out of 4 is 25 out of 100. 75 is three times 25. Older children have bigger feet and also read better, so age can sit behind both.
maths.why_maths: Comparing shares in two groups shows how a third thing, age, can sit behind two things that go together.

maths.problem: A helper reads a tape measure and gets 128 centimetres. Another gets 130 centimetres for the same child. They agree to give the middle value. What is the middle value, and by how much does each reading differ from it?
maths.answer: 129 centimetres. Each reading differs from it by 1 centimetre.
maths.explain: The middle between 128 and 130 is 129, because 128 plus 130 is 258, and half of 258 is 129. 129 minus 128 is 1 and 130 minus 129 is 1.
maths.context: In the Arm Span test, two measurements of the same child may differ by a centimetre or two.
maths.why_maths: A middle value is a fair way to report two readings, and the difference from it tells you the size of the wobble.
