how_we_found_out.story: In 1967, Jocelyn Bell was a research student at Cambridge in England. Her job was to read long paper charts from a new radio telescope that listened to the sky. One day she saw a small strange mark, which she called a bit of scruff. It came back. The team first asked if it was interference from something on Earth, such as a passing car or a radio. Then Bell noticed something clever. The mark returned about four minutes earlier each day by the clock. Things in the sky do that, because the stars rise earlier each day. Machines on Earth follow the clock on the wall. So the mark came from space. Looking closer, the mark was a very regular pulse. The team half-jokingly wondered if it was a message. In fact, it was a new kind of star, now called a pulsar. In 1974 the Nobel Prize for this work went to her supervisor and another senior scientist, and not to her.
how_we_found_out.who: Jocelyn Bell (now Jocelyn Bell Burnell), a research student at Cambridge, with her supervisor Antony Hewish and their team
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Nobody expected a star to pulse so fast and so evenly, so the first guess was that a regular beat must come from machines on Earth. Bell's team showed that the beat followed star time, so it came from far beyond the Earth.

roots.context: We have tested a tumbler, sorted what we saw from what we thought, and learned to ask the question that tells ideas apart. Now we ask what this says about seeing, and about how we know anything.

deep_truth.truth: Everyone beside the tumbler saw the same drops. Some said the water leaked through the steel, and some said it came from the air. What we see is shared. The story we add is ours, and we usually forget that we added it.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'I saw the water leak through' as if the leaking were something we saw. We saw drops. The leaking was a story we added so quickly that it felt like seeing.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Weeping Tumbler, the red water stayed inside and the drops outside were clear. Everyone saw the same drops, and only a question about colour could separate the stories.

three.who_am_i: You tell yourself stories all day about what you see. When a friend does not smile, you think she is cross. The smile was seen. The 'cross' was added.
three.what_is_life: Many beings read the world and guess. A crow turns their head and decides if your hand holds food. A seedling leans towards the light. Living beings act on guesses about what they sense, and they learn when a guess fails.
three.what_is_this_world: The air, the steel, the ice and your eyes took part in one happening. We cut it into 'what I saw' and 'what I think' afterwards. The world did not come with that cut.

roots.thread: The cold tumbler, the air, the drops and your eyes were all part of one happening. Nothing in it came labelled 'observation' or 'explanation'. We make that cut ourselves, so that we can check our stories one at a time. Everything we know comes from bodies meeting the world, and every body adds a little of its own. A bee sees the same flower as you, and in a different way. When we pull the seeing and the story apart and test the story, we are not leaving the world. We are looking at it more carefully.

teachings.teaching: Zhuangzi and his friend Huizi stood on a bridge over a river. Zhuangzi said, 'The fish swim about so freely. They are happy.' Huizi said, 'You are not a fish. How do you know they are happy?' Zhuangzi answered, 'You are not me. How do you know I do not know?'
teachings.link: 'The fish are happy' is a story added to what Zhuangzi saw, which was fish swimming about. Huizi asked the question of an investigator: how do you know? The answer might be a way to check, or it might be an honest 'I do not know'.

teachings.teaching: The hymn of creation asks where everything came from. It ends by saying that perhaps even the one who looks down from the highest heaven knows, or perhaps even that one does not know.
teachings.link: It is very old and it shows honest not-knowing. 'I do not know yet' is where a good question begins, before any story is chosen.

teachings.teaching: The Nyaya school opens with a list of sixteen topics for good enquiry. The list includes doubt and the settling of a question, as well as discussion and the spotting of faulty reasoning.
teachings.link: Doubt comes before settlement. Rival explanations are a kind of doubt, and a deciding question is how to move from doubt to a settled answer.

science.text: Observations can be checked by anyone, while explanations are tested step by step. Scientists keep the two apart when they report results.
People add expectations to what they see, without noticing. Psychologists have shown that what we expect changes what we notice and remember.

other_view.view: No observation is ever free of ideas. What we choose to look at, and the words we use for it, already carry theories. So the line between what I saw and what I think is never sharp. It is a useful habit, but not a clean split.

playtest: Read and walked through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home by a family. Weeping Tumbler: steel tumblers filled with ice and chilled water get fine drops on the outside within 5 to 10 minutes in a humid kitchen, and the drops are clear while the water inside is coloured. In a very dry room or an air-conditioned room, it may take up to 20 minutes, and the steps say what to do then (more ice, breathe on the steel to see mist at once). The warm tumbler stays dry or shows only a faint mist at the start. Colour spilled on the outside makes drops look tinted, so the steps say to wipe the outside dry after pouring. Arm Span: needs six or more people, which a small flat may not have, so the step says to ask neighbours or friends or measure on another day. Measurements wobble by a centimetre or two, and the steps say to write both and not worry. Fridge Light: the phone's own glow lights the video, so the cupboard video is a control.
